name: GPT Researcher (open source deep research with progress callbacks)
what_we_take: The breadth x depth x concurrency research tree with the ResearchProgress callback shape (current/total depth, current/total breadth, current_query, completed/total queries) and skip-failed-branch behaviour, rebuilt around a Person+Claim output instead of a prose report.
why: It is alive (v3.7.0 on 2026-09-26, push 2026-10-10, Apache-2.0, 30.3k stars) and its depth dial (default breadth 4, depth 2, about 5 min and $0.40 per run on o3-mini high, per its docs) maps onto F17, but every stage ends in a 2,000-word report, so per-claim quote and date (F5, K2) and cards that fill in as found (F7) would mean rewriting the planner-to-publisher chain rather than configuring it. Forking a report pipeline to emit people costs more than writing the same tree around our own Person schema, so we copy the control knobs and progress events, not the code. It is the most complete of the four agent loops in this batch, so it replaces open_deep_research as the source of the cheap/strong model split (it already has FAST_LLM, SMART_LLM, STRATEGIC_LLM).
knockout_failed: none as a component; as a discovery option its prose report fails K2 until reworked, which is why it is borrow, not benchmark

facts_checked.claim: Latest release v3.7.0 published 2026-09-26, Apache-2.0, about 30.3k stars, not archived
Deep mode defaults breadth 4, depth 2, concurrency 4; about 5 minutes and $0.40 per run with o3-mini high
ResearchProgress exposes current/total depth, current/total breadth, current_query, completed/total queries; failed queries are skipped
Output supports per-claim quotes or a structured person schema
facts_checked.source: https://docs.gptr.dev/docs/gpt-researcher/gptr/deep_research (describes only the report; no claim-level schema)

beats_or_loses_to: Beats node-DeepResearch as the source for the depth dial and progress events because it already parallelises branches and reports progress; loses to node-DeepResearch on the per-person gap loop, which fits F6 better. Loses to the commercial discovery contenders in other categories as an off-the-shelf benchmark, since it needs rework before it can even be scored on K2.
pricing_terms: Apache-2.0. Cost is LLM and search API usage.
what_it_is: Planner generates sub-questions, execution agents research each, a publisher compiles a report. Deep Research mode runs a tree: breadth (default 4), depth (default 2), concurrency (default 4), about 5 minutes and about $0.40 per run with o3-mini high.

name: Jina node-DeepResearch agent loop (gap queue + token budget + forced answer)
what_we_take: The loop control: a gaps queue fed by a reflect step that dedups sub-questions, actions disabled for the next step when they yield nothing new, a token budget as the stop condition, and a final forced-answer step that must report what is still missing.
why: Each missing claim on a card ('Flemish tie: not found' for Thierry Klein in GS-02, tie type for the five MIT people in GS-10) becomes a gap question, and the budget size becomes the Quick to Deep dial, which serves F17 and gives a deterministic cost per search for the effort-and-quality NFR. The answer-evaluation step (definitive plus references, else stored as a bad attempt and context reset) is the K2/F6 rule that a field stays empty rather than guessed. We copy the control flow (a few hundred lines) instead of running the TypeScript repo, whose last push was 2026-05-01 and whose README calls it still under active development.

facts_checked.claim: Not archived, Apache-2.0, 5.2k stars, last push 2026-05-01
Loop over search, visit, reflect, answer with a gaps queue, token budget and Beast Mode final answer; bad attempts stored and context reset
Actions are disabled for the next step when they produce nothing new
README documents evaluator types or a structured output schema
facts_checked.source: https://github.com/jina-ai/node-DeepResearch README (only says models must support structured output)

beats_or_loses_to: Beats GPT Researcher and deepagents on the one piece FN needs most from an agent loop, turning empty fields into targeted follow-up searches (F6); loses to GPT Researcher on parallel branches and progress reporting, so the two borrowed parts sit side by side, one inside the per-person fill-in step and one at the search level.
pricing_terms: Apache-2.0.
what_it_is: Small TypeScript agent that loops over four actions (search, visit, reflect, answer) against a queue of gap questions until it has a definitive answer with references or runs out of token budget, then a 'Beast Mode' step forces a final answer. Bad attempts are stored and context reset.

name: DeepResearch Bench FACT metric (citation accuracy check)
what_we_take: The FACT procedure and its two numbers (citation accuracy = supported claims / cited claims; effective citations = supported claims per task), applied to FN's stored Claim rows: fetch each source URL with our own fetcher, check the stored quote appears on the page, and have an LLM judge whether the quote supports the claim.
why: The explainability NFR asks that 100% of shown claims carry a source, quote and date, and the POC lesson is that a silent schema break disabled verification for months, so every gold-set run needs an automatic score of whether claims hold up against their pages. FACT already defines that score, but it is built to pull statement-URL pairs out of prose reports and scrapes through Jina with a JINA_API_KEY; FN claims are already structured, so we skip the extraction step and keep the fetch, support judgment and the two metrics. Copying the procedure is hours of work; running the repo as is would add a Jina dependency and a parser we do not need.

facts_checked.claim: FACT extracts statement-URL pairs, dedups, scrapes with Jina (JINA_API_KEY), and an LLM judge decides support; outputs citation accuracy and effective citations
Default FACT judge is gpt-5.4-mini, overridable with FACT_MODEL; latest news item 2026-09-22
Repo alive and licensed
facts_checked.source: https://api.github.com/repos/Ayanami0730/deep_research_bench (Apache-2.0, pushed 2026-09-29, not archived); README badge says MIT, so the licence label is inconsistent but permissive either way

beats_or_loses_to: The only item in this batch that measures claim correctness rather than finding people, so it has no sibling; it beats RACE (report-quality score from the same repo), which FN has no use for since FN shows cards, not reports.
pricing_terms: Free code; LLM judge calls cost tokens.
what_it_is: Benchmark of 100 PhD-level tasks with two scorers. RACE rates report quality. FACT extracts statement-URL pairs, scrapes each cited page and has an LLM judge whether the page supports the claim, reporting Citation Accuracy and Effective Citations per task.

name: DeepWideSearch benchmark (Alibaba)
what_we_take: The three-level table scoring: column F1 on the identifying column (did we find the picked people, our recall), row F1 per entity (are all of a person's fields filled and correct) and item F1 per cell (is each claim, such as tie type, correct), applied to FN's gold-set output.
why: F17 and the effort-and-quality NFR require that a deeper search returns measurably more filled-in, sourced fields, and recall alone cannot show that; row and item F1 give the field-level number per depth, so Quick vs Extended vs Deep can be compared on GS-02 (four Bell Labs people, each with a tie type) and GS-10 (five MIT people, all tie type Belgian). The dataset itself (220 tasks, 15 domains, CC BY 4.0, on Hugging Face as AIDC-AI/DeepWideSearch) adds nothing over our 28 gold cases, and its four failure modes are already covered by K2 (no model memory) and the gap loop borrowed from node-DeepResearch. Best agent average success rate is 2.39% (WebSailor with Claude Sonnet 4), item F1 32.90%, which also sets a realistic expectation that per-cell accuracy, not exact-table success, is the metric to track.

facts_checked.claim: 220 tasks in 15 domains; best average success rate 2.39%; four failure modes named
Metrics include row F1, column F1 and item F1 besides success rate
facts_checked.source: https://arxiv.org/html/2510.20168v1 (Table 2: WebSailor Claude Sonnet 4 row F1 16.88%, item F1 32.90%, column F1 42.01% Avg@4)

name: You.com Research API
what_we_take: The /v1/research endpoint with output_schema set to the FN Person-and-claims schema, run at standard, deep and exhaustive as one bake-off entry, with background:true plus the stream URL for the overnight tier and source_control.boost_domains (e.g. kuleuven.be, ugent.be, imec-int.com) to reach Flanders-based experts.
why: The finding is out of date in the direction that matters: the current API reference documents output_schema (beta, all tiers except lite), background jobs with polling and streaming, and source_control (include, exclude and boost domains, freshness, country), so it can emit Person JSON in one pass at $0.05 to $0.45 per call with published latencies from under 10 s to under 300 s, which is a clean depth ladder for F17. It loses on K2 granularity to a per-field-citation API such as Parallel's Task API: You.com sources carry only URL, title and snippets with no date, and it is not documented that inline citation numbers survive into schema output, so the quote has to be matched to the claim and the date set to the read time by us. Run it head-to-head on the gold set (GS-02 Bell Labs, GS-10 Belgian faculty at MIT) with Exa, Parallel and Tavily before choosing; adopt at most one of them.

name: STORM / Co-STORM perspective-guided questioning
requirements_served: Differentiator: reach into hard groups (Flanders-based experts, low web footprint)
what_we_take: Two prompt steps for the Extended and Deep tiers: (1) STORM's perspective discovery, where the topic is expanded into perspectives (Flemish university alumni, US industrial lab, Belgian francophone university, Flemish research institute such as imec or VIB, US agency, chamber) and each gets its own search queries; (2) Co-STORM's moderator rule of asking new questions from retrieved-but-unused material, turned into a lead queue of names and institutions seen in pages but not yet searched.
why: Single-topic queries miss the hard groups: 18 of the 63 picked people were flown in from Belgium and are found through Flemish institutions, and GS-10 needs a 'Belgian francophone university' perspective (ULiege, UCLouvain, ULB) to surface Lermusiaux, de Wit and Janjevic, while GS-02 needs an 'industrial lab' perspective to reach Bell Labs pages for Baeyens and Vetter. The repo itself is not usable as is: it writes Wikipedia-style long articles, not people with claims, and the code is stale (last commit 2025-09-30, knowledge-storm 1.1.1 on PyPI 2025-09-29, latest README news January 2025). The two steps are about 50 lines of prompt and orchestration on top of whichever search API wins the benchmark, so we copy the method, not the package.

name: Evaluation protocol: pooled recall, dimension ladder, live-web LLM judge
requirements_served: Differentiators: recall, precision, quality for extra time and cost
NFR every search records time and cost
what_we_take: From NewsCatcher, four metrics for every option: pooled recall against the union of verified people from all options, a live-web Claude judge that checks each returned person and claim, a fixed time cap per depth, and $ per true positive. From effiflo, a ladder built from the gold cases (topic, then +place, then +tie, then +ask) on which every returned name is graded on every constraint, with missing evidence counted as not met.
why: Known picks measure recall only. Pooled recall plus the live-web judge give a precision and recall number for the new people every tool finds, and the 3-of-5 target needs that. $/TP and the time cap answer 'deeper must mean better' with one number per depth. The ladder shows where each tool stops working. That matters because FN asks combine topic, place and tie, as in GS-02 (6G + NY/NJ + Flemish) and GS-04 (supply chain + Atlanta + Belgian). Both sources are small (15 event queries; 10 searches per product) and vendor-adjacent, so we copy the method and ignore their rankings.

what_it_is: Two public test designs. NewsCatcher: recall measured against the union of verified results from all providers, a Claude judge checks each result against the live web, each provider gets the same time cap, and cost is reported per true positive. effiflo: a 'ladder' of searches that adds one constraint per rung (role, city, employer type, experience, past employer) and grades every returned name on every constraint.

name: WideSearch benchmark (broad multi-entity table collection)
requirements_served: F17 deeper searches return more people and more filled fields
what_we_take: Two metrics for the FN suite. The first is item-level F1, which scores each claim cell (topic, tie type, availability) separately from row-level correctness. The second is Avg@N next to Pass@N, run 3 to 4 times per option, so run-to-run variance in agentic discovery shows before we choose a tool.
why: FN output is a table of people with claims, which matches WideSearch's task shape. Its leaderboard shows the split we should expect: whole-table success is at most 5.1 (o3 multi-agent), while Claude Sonnet 4 multi-agent reaches Row F1 38.5 and Item F1 62.2. So we judge Deep tier options per row and per claim, never on whole-list completeness, and we keep the rule that every shown row carries a checked claim. Its 200 tasks are not about people, so we do not use them as a second yardstick. The gold set stays the only scoring set.

rerate.verifier_reason: The drop holds. I re-checked the key facts myself. The saved pricing page (probes/i02-docs-pricing.txt) says: "5,000 free search requests per month (shared across all Gemini 3 and newer models), then $14 per 1,000 requests (subject to a daily cap of 1,500 requests per day)". Each query the model runs is billed separately. The live google-search docs (fetched 2026-10-29) show tools=[{"type":"google_search"}] with no domain option. Citations are url_citation (url, title, start_index, end_index) into the model's own answer, with no source snippet and no page date. The .NET and Kotlin GenAI SDK references mark excludeDomains as not supported in the Gemini API. Vertex has exclude only and no include list, so the precedent lane (delegation, mission, chamber and alumni domains only) cannot run on Gemini either way. OpenAI pricing (fetched 2026-10-29) is "$10.00 / 1k calls + Search content tokens billed at model rates". OpenAI does take allowed_domains (up to 100) and has a sources field listing every URL consulted. Its output is still an LLM answer plus URLs, which is the same case as Claude web_search under Not doing, at 10 times Parallel fast's $1 per 1,000. So the duplicate is real: the job (topic or precedent URL leads that FN fetches itself) is the same, the output shape is worse (a few cited URLs, not a ranked list with snippets), and control is weaker (the model picks the queries). The only distinct asset is Google's index. Its gain on the weak groups is unmeasured and no keyless probe exists. It is also unlikely to change the weak-group misses, for a mechanical reason: in GS-22 (Danneels, Flaam, Audenaert, Tuyls), GS-21 (Himpe-Depuydt, Wen, Kegels), GS-24 (Bailet, Curchitser, Rosenwaks) and GS-03 (Vantieghem, Vandenbroucke, Rutten, Vanneste), the picks sit mainly on the event's own post or program. The design already strips those pages as lookup, not discovery, and any index finds them equally. For GS-12 (Kore Yoors) and GS-30 (Pohl, Ertas), FRIS, Exa and Parallel already score. GS-07 and GS-08 are the only plausible Google-index wins, and they stay "expected". Arm D's Perplexity nl sub-arm already tests a second index with a real language filter. One fair counterpoint fails to flip the verdict. The 5,000 free requests a month would make a Gemini benchmark nearly free. But benchmark status needs a credible contender for the production job, and $14 per 1,000 with a 1,500-a-day cap and no include filter rules out production use even if it wins. The judge's conditional fallback is the right shape: 4 prompts on GS-07 and GS-08, only if arms A, B and D all miss Boutelegier, Joris and D'Hulst. One minor rater imprecision: the $25 per 1,000 OpenAI row is web search preview for non-reasoning models, and there search content tokens are free, not billed at model rates. It does not affect the verdict.

name: Claude web search tool + Citations feature (quote-level grounding for our own pipeline)
what_we_take: Run discovery with web_search, then read each candidate page with web_fetch (citations.enabled=true), so every Claim gets a char_location cited_text quote, the URL and retrieved_at as the read date. A second call without citations maps those quotes into the Person/Claim schema, because citations combined with structured outputs returns a 400.
why: This is the only option in the batch that returns an exact supporting span for each claim the model writes. Report-level links (Gemini) or search snippets (Tavily/Brave in the POC) cannot meet '100% of shown claims have URL, quote and date' without a separate matching step. Web fetch costs only tokens (about 2,500 tokens per 10 kB page) and web search costs $10 per 1,000. cited_text is not billed as output tokens. Caveats: web_search cited_text is capped at 150 chars and page_age is the site's last update, not the claim date, so the fetched-page citation is the real quote. Web fetch does not render JavaScript, and it can only fetch URLs that already appeared in context, so the code must pass candidate URLs in a user message or a client tool result.

name: Parallel Ultra deep research loop (code-writing orchestrator with budget awareness)
requirements_served: NFR effort and quality (time and cost recorded per search)
what_we_take: For the Deep tier worker loop: keep fetched pages and the growing candidate table in interpreter variables so only each step's final output re-enters context. Track cumulative LLM and search spend, not a step count, warn as the budget shrinks, and force a synthesis step when the budget runs low.
why: An overnight Deep run will read hundreds of pages. Keeping that in variables instead of the prompt is the fix for context overflow, and a spend-based stop gives F17 its 'time and cost' record and a clean end. Claude's dynamic filtering already filters inside one request (web_search_20260209+), so what we copy is the cross-step state and the budget wrap-up, not the filtering. The hosted Ultra numbers (70% at $0.30, Ultra8x 82% at $2.40 on DeepSearchQA) are vendor-run with no date on the page, so they do not justify adopting the service from this finding. The hosted Task API belongs to a separate benchmark entry.

rerate.verifier_reason:
The drop holds, but on duplication and missing controls, not on a knockout. It passes K1 to K5. K4 only needs one depth, and a task of under 20 minutes fits Extended, so the 60-minute cap does not knock it out. It only rules it out for Deep, which the design caps at 8 h (mvp-tech-reference.md lines 99 and 261).

I re-fetched https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/deep-research live on 2026-10-29 (HTTP 200, last updated 2026-10-13; copy saved in probes/i02-verify/live.html). The Limitations section still says: no structured outputs, no custom function-calling tools (remote MCP only), 60-minute maximum and most tasks under 20. The estimates are still ~$1 to $3 a task for standard and ~$3 to $7 for Max. The saved pricing page bills the agent at standard Gemini token rates plus grounding fees: 5,000 free searches a month, then $14 per 1,000, with a 1,500-a-day cap. It names no budget control. The Interactions API reference confirms that UrlCitation carries only url, title, start_index and end_index, so FN would re-fetch every page for the quote and date, as it does for any search API.

The attack fails on three points:
1. Its one unique asset is Google's index. The same index is reachable more cheaply and under FN's own control through Gemini grounding inside FN's workers. That row is being re-rated now that K6 changed, so if Google coverage matters, that row is where FN gets it.
2. The vendor research tier it would join is deferred in round one (Not doing, line 480: Perplexity Agent API, Exa Agent and others). Those options have output schemas and effort or budget controls, and this one has neither.
3. There is no evidence it finds the weak-group picks. GS-03 and GS-33 (Atlanta, Unilin and Mohawk people) already go through EDGAR, and GS-08 and GS-22 (founders) go through precedent pages. No probe exists for any of the ten weak cases: business GS-03, GS-08, GS-22, GS-33; creative GS-11, GS-12, GS-21, GS-30; low footprint GS-24, GS-31. A probe needs a Gemini key, so a coverage gain cannot be confirmed and counts as not holding.

A prose report also has to be parsed into people before verification, which adds a step and a failure point that the schema-based options do not have.

name: DeepSearchQA (Google DeepMind) set-answer benchmark
requirements_served: NFR effort and quality (deeper must score better)
what_we_take: Use its scoring recipe for the 28-case gold-set run: per case, P = |S∩G|/|S| and R = |S∩G|/|G|. An LLM judge returns JSON with a found/not-found map per gold person plus a list of extra answers, and every run reports the share of 'premature stopping' (low R) and 'hedging' (long lists with low P) results.
why: The paper's judge output (a found map per gold item plus the extra answers) matches what our recall run needs. We only add name-variant matching (Niko/Nikolai), and the extra-answers list is the input for the human precision review. Its two named failure modes give each depth tier two numbers to show that deeper beats quicker. We do not take the 900 prompts: none are people-finding, and the dataset licence is not stated (only the paper is CC BY 4.0).

facts_checked.claim: 900 prompts, 17 fields, names premature stopping and hedging
Scoring is set precision/recall/F1 per prompt with a zero-shot Gemini 2.5 Flash judge returning JSON with a per-gold-item found map and excessive answers
Dataset licence stated
facts_checked.source: arXiv shows CC BY 4.0 for the paper only; Kaggle page not opened

facts_checked.claim: Vendors quote it

beats_or_loses_to: It is the only evaluation item in this batch, so no sibling overlaps. Its set-F1 with an extra-answers list beats a plain recall@k, because the human precision review needs that list of extra people.
pricing_terms: Free dataset.
what_it_is: 900 prompts across 17 fields, most needing an exhaustive list of answers instead of one answer, scored on answer-set precision and recall with an LLM judge. Names two failure modes: premature stopping and hedging with many low-confidence answers.

name: A-MapReduce (agentic MapReduce for wide search)
requirements_served: Reach into Flanders-based experts who travel
what_we_take: For Extended and Deep runs: a planner step turns topic+place into a list of targets (institutions, companies, programs, and Flemish institutions for flown-in experts), parallel map workers each return candidate rows for one target, and a reduce step merges them into the Person table with identifier-first dedup. We skip the experiential-memory part.
why: The gold set rewards splitting by target. GS-02 (6G, NY/NJ) becomes the target 'Nokia Bell Labs Murray Hill', whose people pages name Yves Baeyens, Peter Vetter and Thierry Klein. GS-10 becomes MIT departments, and C-01 to C-03 become imec, KU Leuven and UGent, which a single topic query misses. The abstract reports Item F1 gains of 5.11% to 17.50% over strong baselines on WideSearch and DeepWideSearch, plus 45.8% less run time than multi-agent baselines. The released code (Apache-2.0, 15 stars, last push 2026-03-12) is built on FlashOAgents with o3 or Gemini 2.5 Pro and benchmark-specific runners, so we copy the structure rather than run it. Experiential memory only pays off across many repeat runs, a condition the MVP doc does not state, so we leave it out.

facts_checked.claim: Paper exists, v2 revised 2026-10-23; Item F1 +5.11% to +17.50% with o3/Gemini 2.5 Pro backbones; 45.8% less running time; SOTA on WideSearch and DeepWideSearch
Code released

beats_or_loses_to: It complements the Parallel-style loop: A-MapReduce owns the fan-out by target and the merge into a table, and the Parallel pattern owns each worker's context and budget. Neither duplicates the other. It beats a single long agent loop on the WideSearch-type failure where a single agent stops at the obvious five people, because each target worker covers its own page set.

what_we_take: One POST /agent/runs per search with a Person/Claim outputSchema, effort mapped to the depth dial (low = Quick, high/xhigh = Extended, ultra with budget.maxCostDollars = Deep), input.exclusion fed with the network plus skipped people, and costDollars written to the Search record.

name: Parallel Task API (processor ladder + per-field Basis)
what_we_take: The Basis data shape as FN's Claim record: one entry per field and per list element (dot paths like people.0.tie), each with url, excerpts, reasoning and a high/medium/low confidence, plus our own as_of_date and verified-quote fields.
why: As a discovery tool it duplicates FindAll, which is the same vendor's people-list product with match status, and FindAll's enrichments already run on the Task API. An ultra deep-research report that lists people is a weaker shape than a matched candidate list, and it takes 5 to 25 minutes per run. Run on its own per candidate (core at $0.025), it duplicates the Claude Agent SDK loop, which we control and which can write the date and quote fields Basis lacks. What it adds is a proven per-field, per-list-element evidence layout that maps directly onto F5/F6, so we copy that layout.

It does not duplicate arm D, because it searches a different index, and it aims at the main risk the design names: business and low-footprint picks that general web search misses. One correction to the smoke test. The tool description says to prefer web search for executives and public figures, which describes GS-02 (Bell Labs fellows) and GS-10 (MIT faculty). rerate.verifier_reason:
The benchmark verdict holds, but two facts need correcting first. I re-read the saved probe copies and fetched the live docs on 2026-10-29: people-search.md, pricing.md and overview.md all returned 200.

What I confirmed:
- search_type is one enum with three values (web, fast, people). So people search cannot run at the $1 fast rate.
- max_results goes up to 50 for people search, against 20 for web search.
- The Agent API people_search tool costs $5 per 1,000 invocations.
- A keyless POST returns 401 invalid_api_key.
- Purchase is self-serve. The sales form is optional, for custom pricing only, so K5 passes.
- The Search API tool description says to "prefer search_web" for "executives, leadership teams, or public figures". That backs the judge's correction to the smoke test.

K1 passes. The Search API page itself gives "Machine learning researchers at Stanford" (role plus institution) as a query tip, so a search can start from a topic or institution.

It does not duplicate arm D, because it queries a "dedicated index for individual profiles and employee data". It is not a proven duplicate of Exa's people category either. Exa's structured educationHistory may suit the tie check better, but no data shows Exa finds more gold picks, so only the gold run can rank the two.

It aims at the right gap. The picks plain web search found hardest are thin-footprint business people whose own evidence is a LinkedIn profile:
- Michel Segers (GS-09, Absolem, Charleston)
- Jan Beke (GS-31, OpenAI go-to-market)
- Simon Lemmy (GS-33, UCB US talent lead)
- Philip Vervloesem (GS-03, OMP USA)

A people index is where those should show up, and testing it costs one parameter and under $1. Every gold-case gain is still "expected": nothing was probed and nothing yet beats the incumbents.

Keep the judge's gate:
- Run the smoke test on GS-33, GS-31, GS-09 and GS-03 as well as GS-02 and GS-10.
- Admit it to the full run only if it finds a pick that arms A, B and plain D miss.
- Pick role-plus-company queries ("UCB talent lead US", "Absolem engineering US") over "OMP USA leadership". The vendor's own tool description sends leadership-team questions to web search.
- Read the actual billed price from the smoke-test usage before the full run. The Search API pricing page has no separate price for people search.

rerate.verifier_reason:
The drop holds, but the reason needs fixing. "Duplicates Parallel" is not a clean duplicate on its own terms. Brave runs its own independent index, and the design already keeps A and B as separate arms because their indexes found different picks. So the drop has to rest on recall: Brave is not a credible discovery contender, and the gold set shows that.

I re-checked the key facts on the vendors' own pages on 2026-10-29. Brave Search is $5 per 1,000 with a $5 monthly credit (api-dashboard.search.brave.com/documentation/pricing). Parallel Search fast is $1 per 1,000, with 10 results included (docs.parallel.ai/getting-started/pricing). Arm B (Exa) found 3 of 4 GS-02 picks in the top 10, per the Arms table in mvp-tech-reference.md.

I attacked the drop on the weak groups. After a 19-minute wait, I sent one public Brave results-page query for GS-33 as typed. It returned 200. The top 20 had none of De Cock, Lemmy or Hoferle. The UCB story on globalatlanta.com at rank 11 returned 403 to a page fetch. The metroatlantaceo page at rank 12 is dated 2026, after the event, and names no pick. bacos.us/about at rank 17 names Vervloesem and Vantieghem. Those are GS-03 picks, and that chamber page is already covered by the planned chamber precedent and seed lane, so Brave adds nothing there. The next query, GS-11 as typed and sent 12 s later, returned HTTP 429. I stopped there without retrying, so GS-11, GS-12, GS-21, GS-22, GS-24, GS-30 and GS-31 were not run.

Evidence so far is 1 of 4 picks on GS-02 as typed, against 3 of 4 for Exa, and 0 of 3 on GS-33. Brave found no pick that the incumbent lanes miss.

The free $5 monthly credit would make Brave free at personal volume. That does not matter, because cost is not what limits Quick. The A and B pooled row already tests whether a second index adds anything. The exa-labs harness already has a Brave adapter, so Brave can be re-entered cheaply if arms A and B both fail the precision target. That is a later-round option, not an MVP benchmark slot.

The rater's fact list survives. The two "holds: false" entries are correctly marked as false claims. The one unchecked claim is the AIMultiple latency figure, and the rater already flagged it. Raw files are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-arend-Developer-FN--claude-worktrees-mvp-tech-research-b285c0/f1ac462c-7dec-4c00-b496-a79f3ccba7cd/scratchpad/verify-i04/ (serp-GS-33.html, serp-GS-11.html as the 429 page, parallel-pricing.html, brave-pricing.html).

name: Parallel Task API with Research Basis, Task Groups and source policy
what_we_take: One Task run per candidate with an output schema (tie_type, tie_evidence, employer, location, can_attend, topic_fit), reading each field's basis (citation URL plus excerpts, confidence), mapping null or low confidence to 'not found', running candidates in Task Groups, and pointing tie checks at university and Flemish government domains through source_policy.include_domains.
why: It is the per-person claim verifier FN needs whichever discovery engine wins: every output field returns its own citation excerpt and confidence, so F5's quote and F6's 'missing, never guessed' come from the API instead of our own extraction code, at $5 to $25 per 1,000 people on lite to core. source_policy (200 domains) lets the tie check read kuleuven.be or ugent.be pages, which is how GS-01's Frank Dellaert (KU Leuven 1984-1989) and GS-02's Yves Baeyens (KU Leuven PhD 1997) are settled, and this is the 36-of-99 unsettled-tie gap from earlier research. Dates are not in basis, so the claim date comes from the page read (Parallel Search with after_date or the fetched page), and the customer-terms storage wording needs written confirmation like FindAll.

The pricing page now only redirects, so I used the copy the rater saved the same day: Pro from $98 for 350 records, which is $0.28 a record. On the weak business group, Apify reaches every pick PDL could reach. GS-03 and GS-04: Vervloesem through current employer OMP, HQ in Belgium. GS-33: Lemmy through current employer UCB, HQ in Belgium. GS-03 and GS-33: De Cock through pastCompanies=Unilin or a Belgian school. GS-09: Segers through schools=Vlerick. PDL adds only one filter Apify lacks: a past employer in Belgium for someone with no Belgian school. No weak-group pick needs that. Neither tool helps the BACoS leaders in GS-03 (Vantieghem, Vandenbroucke: US chamber, tie unverified), GS-24 Clauwers (lives in Belgium), GS-31 Beke (tie unverified), or the creative cases GS-11, 12, 21 and 30, where school filters on both tools would be equal. PDL is also worse on three points. Its data is rebuilt monthly while Apify reads live. Its results are sorted by profile completeness, not relevance (Person Search reference). The Base bundle has no headline or about text, while Apify full profiles do. It is also unproven, because every endpoint returned 401 without a key, and the Preview Search key needs a sales call. Its one real advantage is a vendor dataset with no scraper to break. That does not outweigh the rest, since the i39 actor succeeded on 99.6% of 891,686 runs in 30 days. The judge overstated two points that do not change the verdict, listed under failed facts.

rerate.verifier_reason:
The drop holds because the duplicate claim is real. The i39 probe file (i39-build-profile-search.json, harvestapi/linkedin-profile-search build 0.0.289, 2026-10-29) shows the same query shape as the Coresignal lane: searchQuery for the topic, locations for the metro and schools for the Belgian school. It returns education[] schoolName and experience[] start and end dates. The actor's public run stats show 99.6% success over 891,686 runs in 30 days. It also costs less. I checked the actor's own pricing: $0.10 per search page of 25 plus $0.004 per full profile, so a top 20 costs about $0.18 against Coresignal's $2.85 on Pro. Coresignal's 176 ms latency is a vendor claim, and it buys nothing at Quick depth, since collecting even 20 core records ($2.85) is far over the $0.25 cap. A 20-result Search Preview costs about $0.29 on Pro and carries no education field.

I re-fetched these on 2026-10-29. docs.coresignal.com pricing.md shows Pro at $499 for 35,000 credits, a core record at 10 credits (about $0.143) and a 7-day trial of 2,000 credits once per email domain. faq.md says Coresignal "does not access areas that require a login". data-and-compliance.md repeats that. Bright Data's gd_l1viktl72bvl7bjuj0.json still marks position, experience and education "Restricted by LinkedIn since Nov. 13, 2025. Usually empty." The memo23 actor also has a partial-profile price for pages "closed to logged-out visitor", which backs that up. No Coresignal doc I read (core bundle, employee overview, Real-time Employee API dictionary) addresses this restriction or gives fill rates, so the fill-rate risk is unanswered. One point cuts the other way. Education does not change and Coresignal keeps historical records, so an education entry captured before the restriction should still be valid tie evidence. That softens the "stale" part of the argument but not the "empty for new or changed profiles" part, and it is no reason to choose Coresignal over i39, which reads the same field live.

On the weak groups, Coresignal adds no pick that i39 cannot reach with the same filters. GS-03 (De Cock, Vervloesem, Vantieghem, Vandenbroucke in Atlanta) is the best case for a metro plus Belgian-school query, and i39 can run that exact query. GS-22 picks (Danneels, Flaam, Audenaert, Tuyls, Verhamme) and GS-08 Joris are Belgium-based or flown in, so a US-metro filter misses them in both. Creative cases GS-11, GS-12 (Kore Yoors), GS-21 (Steele, Trufelman, Wen) and GS-30 (a London venue, Belgium-based speakers) have no Belgian school to filter on or sit outside a US metro. In low footprint, GS-24 Clauwers is Belgium-based and the other GS-24 picks have unverified ties. GS-31 Beke's tie would only come from his profile's education, and i39 reads that too. GS-33 is not among the 28 scorable cases.

A benchmark needs Coresignal to be a separate contender, and it is not. It is a costlier, possibly emptier copy of the i39 arm. Its only edge, speed or a fallback if Apify breaks, needs a condition the MVP doc does not state. The Bright Data half is dropped on its own docs (fields usually empty, Business Search in beta behind business-email early access).

rerate.verifier_reason: The drop survives. I re-checked every load-bearing fact in the saved vendor docs (probes/i09-md-*.md, pricing HTML, fetched 2026-10-29). (1) No education data. people-enrichment.md and get-complete-person-info.md have no education or school field anywhere. The only degree and major keys sit inside employment_history and are null or empty objects in every example. Apollo therefore cannot type the ties that weak business cases turn on: Segers' Vlerick (GS-09), Bourcy's Vlerick (GS-32), Cardon's Vlerick and UGent (GS-27), D'Hulst's KU Leuven (GS-08). (2) No full names in search. people-api-search.md returns last_name_obfuscated ("first 2 characters, asterisks, last character") and no linkedin_url, so every candidate costs an enrichment credit before it can be matched or carded. (3) The past-employer filter duplicates i39. The q_organization_domains_list filter ("current employer or a previous employer", up to 1,000 domains) is real. But i39's public build schema (harvestapi/linkedin-profile-search) offers currentCompanies, pastCompanies, locations and schools in one query, and its full profiles return education[] and dated experience[]. For GS-03 (Vervloesem via omp.com, De Cock via unilin.com), GS-33 (Lemmy via ucb.com) and GS-22 (Televic, Aptly, Intrinsic ID, Netalux), i39 gets the same employer-plus-metro search and also supplies the tie. Apollo's only extra is 0-credit search over 1,000 domains in one call, while i39 costs $0.10 per 25-profile page. That is a cost difference on a few dozen calls, not a requirement Apollo serves better. (4) No gain in the weak groups. The creative picks (GS-11 Savonie, Vandycke, Altenhaus; GS-12 Kore Yoors; GS-21 Wen, Kegels; GS-30 architects) are freelancers, artists and small practices with no employer domain for a B2B sales index to key on. The low-footprint picks gain nothing either. GS-31 Jan Beke could come up via openai.com plus San Francisco, but Apollo cannot supply the missing tie. GS-24 has no employer anchor. No incumbent miss is clearly recoverable only through Apollo. (5) API access is unclear. The pricing FAQ says "API access is available on Custom plans" and the Enterprise offer is "Contact for pricing". rate-limits.md lists Free, Basic and Professional limits. Under K5 a sales call fails, so per-plan API access is unconfirmed and counts against it. (6) Clearbit/HubSpot Breeze fails K1: it only enriches existing CRM records, and the Clearbit free tools are gone. Nothing in the rater's benchmark case beats i39 plus the company-first planner, so drop is right. A benchmark would spend $49 to measure a lane that i39 covers in a superset.

Fits MVP as a Deep/Extended-tier claim source for US-listed company officers, directors and Form D founders, with dated, citable accession numbers (strong for F5 dated sourced claims). Hit rate on the gold set by name is about 3 of 20 (15 percent), consistent with the rater's earlier result; it only finds people who sign SEC filings (Section 16 officers/directors, Form D related persons, S-1/proxy bios). Academics, consultants, chamber staff and foreign private issuers (Nokia, Televic) are invisible. probe.notes:
Status checked 2026-10-28: PyPI edgartools 5.62.1 uploaded 2026-10-23 (5 days old, alive); license MIT (PyPI metadata and README); README says no API key, no vendor quota, honors SEC fair-access 10 req/s, 'maintained by one person' (single-maintainer risk); has local MCP server in the `ai` extra (tools seen in installed source: edgar_company, edgar_search, edgar_text_search, edgar_filing, edgar_read, edgar_proxy, edgar_ownership, edgar_screen, edgar_compare, edgar_fund, edgar_monitor, edgar_notes, edgar_trends) plus a hosted paid platform edgar.tools; README says no feature is removed from the library. I did NOT run the MCP server (needs the `mcp` extra); only inspected the installed source. GitHub API was rate limited (stars, last push not checked). SEC requires a declared User-Agent: I used a placeholder identity string; FN needs a real contact email in set_identity.

How it fits the MVP: it is a free, key-free enrichment and tie-discovery source for US corporate leaders and boards, not a topic-to-expert search. Use 1: after another stage names a person, EFTS name search plus proxy/Form D gives dated, sourced claims (role, employer, education, years), which suits F5 dated claims and the tie type. Use 2: reverse tie search ('KU Leuven', 'Ghent University', 'Vlerick', 'Katholieke Universiteit Leuven' in DEF 14A, 10-K, S-1) finds Flemish-educated directors and executives the delegation has not listed, e.g. De Backer, Vandebroek. Matches the gold pattern of GS-03, GS-23, GS-27, GS-28 (business leaders) and not academic or government cases (GS-05, 06, 10, 12, 13, 15, 16, 30 will not appear).

Limits seen in the data: (1) EFTS gives no snippet, so every hit needs a 3-request filing open and a text search for the person; hit lists skew to old filings (2001-2012 common). (2) Surname search is noisy: 'Dellaert' 888 hits, 'Vanholder' hit a different person; must filter by quoted full name plus company. (3) Form D related-person address is the issuer's address: Sweldens shows Bethesda MD (7735 Old Georgetown Road), not NJ, so it is a weak base signal; edgartools' related_persons returns names only, address is only in primary_doc.xml. (4) Sweldens also matches a second issuer, TUBE Inc (Chelmsford MA, Form D 2014-06-03, 2015-10-06); I did not open it. (5) Coverage excludes private-company staff, non-exec employees (Vanholder at Nvidia), foreign filers using 20-F/6-K (Nokia's Vetter, Baeyens), academics.

Cost note: install pulls pandas, pyarrow, numpy; for FN it may be lighter to call efts.sec.gov and the Archives with plain HTTP (same endpoints, e.g. https://efts.sec.gov/LATEST/search-index?q=%22KU+Leuven%22&forms=DEF+14A) and borrow edgartools only for Form D and proxy parsing. probe.name: Biblio UGent (REST search, OAI-PMH, SRU, per-person export)

Split by ORCID: 978 records for the EE professor (ugent_id 801000632981, ORCID 0000-0001-9948-9157, affiliation UGent>TW>TW05, years 1992-2026), 223 for a homonym dentist (ORCID 0000-0001-5208-5630, ugent_id 919015140185, affiliation UGent only), 42 neither. probe.known_picks_found: "3 of 9 tested. Luc Martens (GS-29): found, with the caveat that the defense is dated 1991-12-11, not 1990. Peter Vetter (GS-02): found, 1991 dissertation. Serhat Yildirim (GS-06): found, via a journal article (his only record). Missed: Han Vanholder (KU Leuven alum, expected miss), Amaury Hellebuyck (student, no record). Jeroen Dewulf (GS-05): wrong person, a UGent veterinary epidemiologist with the same name. Wim Sweldens, Yves Baeyens and Frank Dellaert were not queried because they are KU Leuven alumni (UGent-only index)."
probe.latency_and_calls: "21 HTTP calls (budget 60). Typical 0.12-0.41s. Slowest was 0.69s for a 14.4 MB response (1,589 records). The largest single response, with all 1,243 Martens records, took 0.71s. Two calls returned HTTP 500: Lucene field syntax inside q (year:[1985 TO 1991] and author:\"...\") and the non-export /publication?format=json. No rate-limit headers or throttling seen. The server sets a biblio.session cookie, which is not needed. The server date header read 28 Oct 2026, so the service is live."
probe.tie_signal: "Yes, and it is the strength of this source, with a homonym caveat. (1) Luc C. Martens, dissertation, defense {location: 'Gent', date: '1991-12-11'}, publisher 'RUG. Faculteit Toegepaste Wetenschappen. Laboratorium voor elektromagnetisme en acustica', promoter P. Lagasse, handle http://hdl.handle.net/1854/LU-8556630, record _id 8556630, date_updated 2026-03-31. Title is 'Enkele bijdragen tot een multi-kanaalshyperthermiesysteem...'. This record has NO ugent_id, ORCID or affiliation (affiliation: null), so linking it to the professor needs name plus topic (his 978 later records on EM exposure and antennas, ORCID 0000-0001-9948-9157) and is not an id join. A second 'Luc C. Martens' dissertation (1987, ESR of tooth enamel, Faculty of Medicine, _id 8543546) belongs to the dentist homonym. (2) Peter Vetter, dissertation defense {Gent, 1991-01-01}, promoter Herman Pauwels, Lab voor elektronica en meettechniek, handle http://hdl.handle.net/1854/LU-8561322. Here the dissertation author does carry ugent_id 919017229931, shared with 1996-2002 passive-optical-network papers (e.g. co-authors F. Fredricx, X.-Z. Qiu), so the id join works and fits the gold note (Ghent PhD, then Alcatel). (3) Serhat Yildirim, ugent_id 802003423732, no ORCID, affiliation path UGent>GE>GE39 (Department of Public Health and Primary Care), 2024 article in International Journal of Medical Education, DOI 10.5116/ijme.6712.35da, handle http://hdl.handle.net/1854/LU-01JHN9C7PMJ1KJ0BNXKT5QGW9N, record created 2025-01-15. This satisfies URL plus date plus affiliation field, but it says nothing about his degree, Harvard or Fayat. No data on KU Leuven, VUB, UAntwerp or imec past affiliations: the index only covers UGent."
probe.notes:
Raw evidence is in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-arend-Developer-FN--claude-worktrees-mvp-tech-research-b285c0/478e8fad-29e6-49fd-acaa-35357605f17f/scratchpad/research/probes/biblio/ (lm.json, sy.json, d5.json, n_Vetter.json, n_Dewulf.json, ai.json, ow.json).

SCORING against the planned hit rule (URL + date + defense/affiliation field as quote): GS-29 Martens is a hit on the dissertation (defense Gent, 1991-12-11) but with a conflict. The gold set says PhD 1990, Biblio says defended 11 Dec 1991, so the gold tie text should be checked or the date dropped. GS-06 Yildirim is a hit. Peter Vetter (GS-02) is a hit with a clean id join. That makes 3 of 3 UGent-linked people found with Gent-defense or UGent-affiliation evidence.

WHAT THE API IS (observed):
- /publication/export?q=...&format=json returns JSON lines, one record per line, with no paging needed for a person. limit=N and year=YYYY and type=dissertation work as separate URL params. q=type:dissertation returns 0 results silently, and Lucene field or range syntax inside q gives HTTP 500.
- Record fields seen: author[] {name, first/last_name, ugent_id[], orcid_id, affiliation[{ugent_id, path[], name}]}, year, type, title, keyword[], doi, handle (a stable URL), date_created, date_updated, language, promoter[], defense {date, location}, publisher.name (lab or faculty for dissertations).
- 48% of author slots in the topic probes have no ugent_id (457 of 951 for AI, 428 of 1,308 for offshore wind), only a name, no affiliation or country. Dissertation authors have affiliation null.
- OAI-PMH Identify works: repository 'Ghent University Institutional Archive', earliestDatestamp 2017-04-20, adminEmail libservice@ugent.be, deletedRecord persistent. SRU works and returns MODS 3.3. I did not check license or terms-of-use text, rate-limit policy, or whether the OAI harvest has set or date filters. A bulk ORCID-keyed harvest would need that checked first.

HOMONYM RISK (the main finding for the pipeline): a name-only query returns the wrong people. 'Luc Martens' mixes an EE professor (978 records) with a dentist (223). 'Jeroen Dewulf' returns 610 records for a UGent veterinary epidemiologist (ugent_id 801001256007, ORCID 0000-0001-9843-5990, faculty CA05, keywords biosecurity, pigs, poultry). The Berkeley Dutch-studies professor in GS-05 is not in Biblio at all, so a naive match would invent a false UGent tie. 'Vanholder' returns only Raymond Vanholder (nephrology). The usable rule is: accept a tie only when an ORCID or ugent_id is already known from another source (person page, ORCID, OpenAlex), or when the dissertation title and lab match the person's field.

TOPIC DISCOVERY: it works for finding UGent-affiliated experts but not for US-based ones. For 'offshore wind' the top authors by record count were Wim De Waele (TW08, ORCID 0000-0002-7196-3328, 49), Bruno Stuyts (TW15, 33), Jeroen De Kooning (TW08, 24), Lieven Vandevelde (TW08, 24), Peter Troch (TW15, 22), Jan Vanaverbeke (WE11, 22) and Steven Degraer (WE11, 20). These are all Belgium-based, so they are flown-in candidates, not 'near Boston'. The 16 offshore-wind dissertations (2013-2025, each with a defense date and a Gent venue) list alumni such as Jan Reubens, Jolien Buyse and Nicolas Quartier, who may now work abroad, but Biblio gives no current employer or location. For 'AI' (2025, 200 records) the top authors were Lennart Jans (GE32, 18), Bernard De Baets (LA26, 15), Tony Belpaeme (TW06, 8), Dick Botteldooren, Tijl De Bie and Sam Leroux. De Baets, Belpaeme and De Bie are plausible keynote candidates for GS-29, but ranking was by record count, not relevance; I did not test sort by relevance. Luc Martens (the gold pick) did not appear in the top 10 of the 2025 AI sample.

PRAGMATIC USE FOR THE MVP: take it as a tie-verification and UGent-roster tool, not a discovery source for US people. Given a name plus ORCID (or a name plus a field), it returns dated, URL-backed claims: 'defended PhD at Ghent University on <date>, promoter X, lab Y' (a handle URL, a date_updated and a defense field to quote) or 'UGent affiliation path UGent>faculty>department' on a dated publication. It costs under 1s per call, with no key and no account. Its coverage limit is that it only sees UGent, so KU Leuven, VUB, UAntwerp and imec ties (most of the gold-set Flemish picks) have to come from other sources. Because the existing rating was not given to me, I mark the verdict as 'confirms' (useful narrow tie-evidence source, with the homonym trap).

name: Undermind deep search (clarify, citation chase, discovery curve)
what_we_take: The discovery-curve test: for every depth, log the gold-set picks found against time spent and cost, and treat a depth whose curve does not rise as a failed depth. Also the rule that resubmitting a search continues from its stored results instead of starting over (F2 reopen-and-deepen).
why: It searches papers only. The homepage never mentions finding people, and no API is listed, so it cannot be a FN discovery source or a gold-set contender. Its published curve (64% recall at 5 min, 73% at 10 min, vs 29 to 39% for general agents, 23 queries, judged by the vendor's own GPT judge) is the clearest ready-made shape for our 'deeper must mean better' NFR: recall@time per depth on the 28 cases. Citation chasing to co-authors adds nothing here, because we would rebuild it from OpenAlex co-authorship, not from Undermind.

name: Clay waterfall enrichment and Claygent conditional runs

rerate.verifier_reason:
The drop holds as a duplicate. The judge's wording has two errors, and neither changes the outcome. I re-read apidocs.pearch.ai/reference/post_v2-search.md and pearch.ai/pricing on 2026-10-29 (saved to scratchpad/v11/doc.md).

1. Pearch can do more than the judge says. search_requirements is natural-language text with a must_have flag. It is not an exact filter. Pearch also has a separate custom_filters parameter with universities, locations, companies, titles, industries and spoken languages. So in one call it combines semantic topic matching with hard school and metro filters and per-requirement insight quotes.

2. That combination is still covered. i39's harvestapi profile-search already pairs a free-text searchQuery with the locations, schools and currentCompanies filters. It costs $0.10 per page of 25 profiles plus $0.004 per full profile, against Pearch's $0.04 to $0.08 per candidate. i34 (Exa people) covers the semantic-only shape.

3. No weak-group case shows a gain.
- GS-03, GS-33 (Vervloesem, Vandenbroucke, De Cock, Lemmy), GS-08 (Joris, D'Hulst) and GS-22 (Audenaert, Tuyls, Flaam): a metro plus Belgian-school filter finds these. i39 runs that filter more cheaply. Exa people found only Vantieghem in 5 GS-03 phrasings, so the gap is real. i39 already fills it.
- GS-31 (Jan Beke): his tie is unverified, so a school filter cannot surface him. A semantic query on AI and media in LA is what i34 already runs.
- Creative cases GS-11, GS-12, GS-21, GS-30: the picks are Kore Yoors, Steele, Kegels, Wen, Pohl and Ertas. Their evidence is event posts and biographies, and title-ranked recruiter search does not reach "Jan Yoors" or "Antwerp style".
- GS-24 (Clauwers, Rosenwaks, Curchitser): an ocean-governance panel. Nothing points to Pearch over Exa people here.

4. Recall is unmeasured. The keyless calls got a 401 from the MCP endpoint and a 403 from the REST API. So every "expected" pick in the rating is unconfirmed and counts as not holding.

5. Pearch cannot serve Quick. Quick with 30 candidates costs $1.20 even with insights on, and $0.04 a candidate allows only about 6 candidates under the $0.25 cap. The fast type also takes up to 50 s.

The rater found no gold pick that both kept arms would miss, so Pearch is a third LinkedIn-index arm with no case of its own. If i39 fails on breakage or account limits, re-open Pearch as its replacement. Do not run it beside i39.

Smaller corrections to the record:
- The pricing page now says the $10 prepaid package auto-renews.
- The docs give 60 search requests a minute. The rater's probe summary said 120, which is the cached-reload limit.

rerate.judge_note: Borrow the trait scheme from SearchTraitV1 and SearchTraitScoreV1, which I confirmed in i12-openapi.json. The Candidate ranker splits the question into short traits and scores each candidate 0, 0.5 or 1 per trait, with an evidence quote tied to an FN claim id. The total is the sum minus a penalty per zero trait, and the fit label follows from the scores: all evidenced, some missing, or topic at 0. rerate.verifier_reason:
Checked on 2026-10-29, the vendor facts hold. I re-fetched happenstance.ai/pricing: Free costs $0, Pro is $30 a month or $24 billed yearly, and the page says "API & MCP use separate credits". The API introduction and get-usage docs give credit counts only, and they send buyers to happenstance.ai/integrations/keys, which needs a login. No dollar price per credit is published. In the live openapi.json, search_everyone is a boolean with no description, and weighted_traits_score is "sum of trait scores minus penalties for traits scored zero". SearchTraitScoreV1 is a score of 0, 0.5 or 1 plus an evidence string. The vendor guide sends "cold discovery across the public web" to Lessie. So as a discovery source it is rightly not adopted or benchmarked.

The borrow fails on duplication. The judge note says "FN's current design has only RRF plus a Sonnet ordering with free-text reasons". That is false. mvp-tech-reference.md already borrows the same idea from three sources:
- Ranker and cards: "Good match, potential fit or not a match from claim coverage, with one row per criterion" (Juicebox).
- Claim extractor: "A verdict per criterion of yes, no or unclear" (Exa Websets).
- Eval runner: "Each ask split into criteria, each graded 0, 0.5 or 1" (PeopleSearchBench).
- Query parser: chips used as live ranking criteria (SeekOut).

The fit label the judge credits to Happenstance ("all evidenced, some missing, topic at 0") is the Juicebox borrow already in the design. The evidence-quote-per-claim-id link is FN's own claim model. That leaves only "sum minus a penalty per zero trait". The vendor does not publish the penalty size, and no trait weights exist despite the field name. That is a one-line scoring rule, not a component worth its own borrow row. It can go into the Juicebox ranker line if wanted.

The gold-case benefits are all "expected", with no probe. On GS-03 the Juicebox criterion rows plus SeekOut chips already separate De Cock and Vervloesem from generic Atlanta executives. On GS-09 a zero penalty would hurt: a "US-based" trait scores Ben Troch 0, because his current LinkedIn base is Diegem, Belgium, so the penalty demotes a gold pick. The rubric defines drop as "duplicates a better option". The Juicebox, Websets and PeopleSearchBench borrows already own this responsibility, and a second owner for it in the ranker would drift. So the verdict is drop.
rerate.settled_note: Settled by me: the verifier showed the trait scheme duplicates borrows already in the design (Juicebox fit label, Websets per-criterion verdicts, PeopleSearchBench 0/0.5/1 scoring), and the zero-trait penalty is unspecified.

rerate.verifier_reason: The drop holds because Diffbot duplicates a better option. The rater's main argument is that Diffbot is "the only option in reach" that can search by school x residence x employer. That is false. The i39 benchmark actor, harvestapi LinkedIn Profile Search (No Cookies), takes the same query in its input schema: schools, locations, currentCompanies, pastCompanies, currentJobTitles and companyHeadquarterLocations (probes/i39-build-profile-search.json, read 2026-10-29). It costs $0.004 per profile (PRICE_PER_DATASET_ITEM). Diffbot costs about $0.03 per entity (25 credits on the $299/250,000-credit Startup plan, confirmed on diffbot.com/pricing 2026-10-29). That is about 7x the price, and the Apify actor reads LinkedIn's own index rather than an undisclosed crawl ("Everywhere on the public web"). The actor is maintained and works: modified 2026-10-29, 888,075 of 891,686 runs succeeded in 30 days. It also has a filter Diffbot lacks, companyHeadquarterLocations=Belgium. That filter hits the employer-tie cases directly: GS-22 Tuyls, Audenaert and Flaam (Intrinsic ID, Aptly, Netalux), GS-03 Vervloesem (OMP, Antwerp) and GS-09 Segers (Absolem). The school filter covers GS-32 Bourcy (Vlerick) and Bolsens-Peetermans (Karel de Grote), GS-01/GS-29 Vanholder (KU Leuven + NVIDIA) and GS-23 Dessein and Burggraeve. So every gold case the rater lists is equally reachable through i39, at lower cost, without a $299 month. In the weak groups Diffbot adds nothing named. The creatives (GS-11 Vandycke, Kegels; GS-12 Kore Yoors; GS-21 Wen; GS-30 Pohl, Ertas) and the low-footprint cases (GS-24 Clauwers; GS-31 Beke, Weaver) have no school x region x employer record the rater could point to. Diffbot's only extra field, nationalities, is inferred, and no source says it covers these people. Academics (GS-02 Baeyens and Vetter, GS-10) are already found by OpenAlex. K2 is no longer a differentiator now that vendor records meet it. Per-fact origins stay unconfirmed: the origin concept doc says each fact comes from origins but shows no per-fact shape. A keyless probe was refused with 401 on both the DQL and MCP endpoints, so the rater produced no evidence that would put Diffbot ahead of i39. Checked myself on 2026-10-29: the diffbot.com/pricing plans and credit costs (hold), the Apify actor's input schema, price and run stats in the saved i39 probe files, and the Diffbot origin and person docs in probes/i37-*.

rerate.judge_note: Duplicates the Tie typer's employer-postcode rule (design step 9) on every gold case it was tested on. Both probe wins come from employers whose own pages already give a Flemish seat. introw.com (fetched 2026-10-29) shows "Dok-Noord 4E 102, 9000 Ghent, Belgium" for GS-18 Geamanu. netalux.com says "Our headquarters have moved to Beringen" for GS-22 Flaam. So the incumbent gives the same flemish label from the same input, since Staatsblad also needs the employer's legal name. I checked the one case where the postcode rule is weak, GS-30 Johan Anrys at 51N4E, which has a Brussels seat. One keyless POST to rech_res.pl returned 16 deeds. The 2005 founding deed 05048917 is an image-only scan, and tesseract OCR names "Johan Jozef Julienne ANRYS, architect" as co-founder with a Brussels-region residence and no birthplace. That leaves Anrys Belgian/unverified, the same as the postcode rule. The Leuven birthplace for Flaam is the only extra fact, and it does not change his label. In return FN would pay days of build: a form adapter, OCR on scans (3 of the 7 PDFs read across both probes had no text layer) and a redaction pass for national register numbers, birth dates and home addresses. Staatsblad Monitor and the NBB CBSO API fail K5 (account sign-up), as the rater found. Evidence: scratchpad/rerate/judge-belgian/ej-51n4e.html, 05048917.ocr.txt, netalux.html, introw.html.
rerate.verifier_reason: The drop fails on the one case the judge used to rule out extra value. The judge's own scan of the 51N4E founding deed 05048917 (Bijlagen 04/04/2005) names Anrys with a Flemish residence, not a Brussels one. I cropped ocr-05048917-1.png and read the line myself. It says "Johan Jozef Julienne ANRYS, architect, wonende te Herent". Herent is in Flemish Brabant, so this is the Flemish Region. Swinnen (Sint-Jans-Molenbeek) and Persyn (Schaarbeek) are the co-founders with Brussels addresses, and the judge seems to have read their lines as his. The deed puts the company seat at Kooimijnenkaai 82, 1080 Brussel, so the employer-postcode rule (design step 9) can only give Anrys belgian or not found. The Staatsblad deed gives a dated, quoted Flemish residence claim for GS-30, a weak creative-group pick that gold marks "unverified". So the claim that it duplicates the incumbent "on every gold case it was tested on" is false. The cost is real but bounded. It is a form-POST adapter, OCR (Docling is already in the stack) and a redaction pass that keeps only the municipality. Staatsblad Monitor and the NBB CBSO API do fail K5 on account sign-up, as both the rater and the judge found. Neither belongs in the adoption. I narrow the adoption to the official ejustice Bijlage Rechtspersonen, run as an Extended/Deep tie step. It runs only when the employer is a Belgian company whose postcode does not already give a Flemish tie, which means seats in Brussels or Wallonia and persons tied by personal company. That scope also cuts most of the lookups. The rater overstated the benefit. Hellebuyck (TechWolf, Ghent), Bovijn (Polysense, Ghent), Danneels (Televic, Izegem), Vanneste (De Halve Maan, Bruges) and Joris (Twikit, Antwerp) all work for employers with Flemish seats. For them the postcode rule already gives flemish, so the deed adds only evidence, not a new label. Flaam (GS-22) is the same case: Netalux has its seat in Beringen. It does not discover people, since rech.pl has no person or topic field, so it adds no picks to discovery for GS-03, GS-08, GS-11, GS-21, GS-24, GS-31 or GS-33. Its proven gain is one weak-group label change (GS-30 Anrys, unverified to flemish), plus a firmer personal tie for Flaam. It is the only keyless official source that ties a person to a place in Flanders when the employer's seat sits outside the Flemish Region.

The verifier read the 51N4E founding deed: "ANRYS, architect, wonende te Herent" gives GS-30 a dated Flemish residence the employer-postcode rule cannot give; Flaam (GS-22) gets "geboren te Leuven". what_we_take: The role-based grading recipe (an LLM judge fetches each returned page and checks it against the query criteria, score = share of matching results) plus the MIT-licensed provider adapters (Exa, Perplexity, Parallel, Brave, Tavily), wired to a gold-set loader so every discovery option is pre-screened the same way before human review.
why: The repo exa-labs/benchmarks is MIT, ships data/people.jsonl (1,400 queries) and adapters for exactly the search APIs FN will compare, which saves writing a comparison harness from scratch. Its 1,400 queries are generic role/geo lookups with no Flemish/Belgian/Dutch tie, so the dataset itself does not replace the 28 gold cases; only the judge and adapters carry over. A page-fetching judge also checks the K2 promise (the cited page actually supports the claim), which a recall@k score on known picks cannot.

key_probe_plan: The owner creates a free Sixtyfour account and key (64 credits, no payment) and keeps the key in the Keychain as SIXTYFOUR_API_KEY. Step 1: one GET /search/filter-capabilities?mode=people to confirm that education (school name) and position start and end dates are in the record; if not, dated vendor-record claims fall back to the read date. Step 2: Deep Search in people mode with output_mode query_only and max_results 20 on the hard-group business and low-footprint cases GS-02, GS-03, GS-08, GS-22, GS-31, GS-32 and GS-33. Run each as the question as typed and as one rewrite that names the education and the place, such as 'people who studied at KU Leuven, Ghent University or Vlerick working in telecom in New Jersey'. That is 7 cases x 2 phrasings x 20 results = 28 credits. Step 3: run the same 14 queries on Exa with category=people under the existing Exa key, so the two LinkedIn indexes meet head to head. Score picks in the top 20 by full name with the duplicate rule, apply the held-out rule (a record that does not mention the event), check the tie label from the record's education field, and log time per search against the 15 min cap. The remaining 36 free credits cover the other 21 cases at about 17 results each. If Sixtyfour beats Exa people on held-out recall outside the bootstrap interval, it becomes the LinkedIn-index lane at Extended, and its dollar price per credit is then read from the billing page before any paid plan.

rerate.verifier_reason:
Neither stated ground for the drop holds as a knockout.

(1) "Unpriced" overstates the gap. I re-read docs.sixtyfour.ai/guides/credits-and-pricing.md on 2026-10-29, and the live copy matches the saved probe. It publishes self-serve plans (Free 64 credits a month, Individual 100, Starter 1,200, Growth 5,000), a credit price for every operation (Deep Search and Filter Search cost 0.1 credit per result) and a $50 minimum top-up, with the rate "shown before you buy". Upgrades happen in the dashboard, so there is no sales call and K5 passes under the settled rule. The dollar rate per credit is not on the vendor site today: www.sixtyfour.ai/pricing returns 404, and the Wayback CDX shows 404 from 2026-08-04. It was published until at least 2026-06-25. The archived page (saved as probes/i35-verify-wayback-pricing-20260625.html) lists Individual at $24 a month ($0.24 per credit), Starter at $264 ($0.22 per credit) and top-ups at $0.30 per credit. That bounds production cost at about $0.02 to $0.03 per result, or about $0.60 for a 20-result search. That is roughly 85 times Exa's $7 per 1,000 searches and counts hard against value at Extended. But the benchmark pass (28 cases x 20 results = 56 credits) costs $0 on the free plan, so cost per held-out pick for the benchmark can be computed and is zero. The missing dollar rate is a value penalty to settle from the billing page before any paid plan, not a reason to skip the benchmark.

(2) It does not duplicate i34 (Exa people). Both are LinkedIn-derived indexes, but Exa's search reference (exa.ai/docs/reference/search, read 2026-10-29) says the people category rejects excludeDomains and the published-date filters and lists no company or location filter. Sixtyfour has Filter Search keyed on the LinkedIn company ID (currentCompanies.company.companyId) and a 5 to 200 mile location radius on /search/query. Those are exactly the weak business picks' shape: an employee of a Belgian firm's US arm near a city, such as Vervloesem at OMP USA in Atlanta (GS-03), Simon Lemmy at UCB (GS-33) and the Televic, Netalux, Aptly and Intrinsic ID panelists in California (GS-22). The round-2 sweep found 0 of 7 GS-03 picks company-first on web search. Exa people cannot express that query, so it is not the "better option" a duplicate drop needs. Several benchmark contenders per group are allowed. Only adopt is limited to one per group of siblings.

Gains should be confined to business. De Cock (GS-03, GS-33) is already found by EDGAR. GS-31 is already 4 of 4 held-out on Exa. The creative cases (GS-11, GS-12, GS-21, GS-30) and the marine case (GS-24) are unlikely wins for a LinkedIn index. Treat those as expected, not probed.

The open risks belong in the head-to-head run, not in the verdict. The self-reported R@1 of 90.4% is on role-plus-city queries graded by GPT-5.4. Education and position dates are undocumented without a key (the docs mention no education field), so Bourcy and Herdewyn (GS-32) and D'Hulst (GS-08) may not get a tie label from the record. The default max_results is 1,000, so the run must set max_results=20 or it uses the free credits on a single search.

Keep the rater's key probe plan, add Filter Search by company ID plus radius for GS-03, GS-22 and GS-33, and score held-out recall against Exa people on the same queries.

key_probe_plan: Needs an account that the owner creates (trial credits, then Basic at $99 a month for 1,000 credits). Run `lessie find-people --query "<question as typed>" --target-count 30` and one synonym rewrite on 9 cases: GS-09, GS-08, GS-31, GS-32, GS-18, GS-01, GS-29, GS-04 and GS-03. That is 18 calls at 20 credits, or 360 credits, about $36 at the Basic rate. For each call, log elapsed_seconds, partial and points_deducted. Match people to picks by full name under the duplicate rule. Then run `enrich-people` with the LinkedIn URL of each found pick, at 1 credit each. Check whether the record has position dates, for dating claims, and education, for ties such as Segers at Vlerick, Vanholder at KU Leuven and Troch with Belgian law degrees. Run the same 9 cases on the Exa people category with the arm B key. Decision rule: Lessie becomes the LinkedIn lane only if it finds at least 2 more held-out picks than Exa people on these cases, its records carry dated position fields, and calls stay under $2. Otherwise it is dropped as a duplicate of the cheaper option.

rerate.judge_note: It duplicates i34 at about $2 a call, against $0.047, and needs a $99 a month subscription with credits that expire. It is a black-box agent with a 60 s cap that FN cannot steer with school or domain lists. Its documented response has no position dates or education, so the dated ties for GS-09 Segers and GS-01 Vanholder are unconfirmed. Its only quality evidence is the vendor's own PeopleSearchBench, which I could not confirm. The public directory held 0 of 99 gold picks, which says nothing for or against.
rerate.verifier_reason:
The drop holds as a duplicate of a better option. It does not rest on a knockout. Under the new rules Lessie passes K1, K2 (vendor record, dated by the read date if needed), K4 and K5 (self-serve Stripe plans). I re-read https://lessie.ai/pricing on 2026-10-29: Basic $99 a month (struck-through $199) for 1,000 credits, 1 concurrent task, find_people 20 credits ($1.19 a request at the Max rate), unused credits do not roll over, and only Enterprise goes through email sales. The cli-reference.md and SKILL.md on GitHub confirm the query is natural language, the cap is 3 tool calls and 60 s, and the response shape has people, sources_used and strategy_used but no per-claim URL, quote or date. The repo was last pushed 2026-07-01 (34 stars) and @lessie/cli is at 0.11.0, published 2026-06-24.

The duplicate is real. SKILL.md says B2B mode searches "professional databases (LinkedIn-based)", which is the same data class as Exa's people category (i34). The i34 probe (i34-summary-raw.txt) ran that category in 1.4 to 4.4 s. It returned Vetter and Baeyens for GS-02 and Vantieghem for GS-03, with LinkedIn URLs, a pub date and education text (KU Leuven, Ghent University) that FN can quote as a tie. That is the tie evidence Lessie's find_people response does not document. Exa's pricing page gives $7 per 1k Auto searches plus $1 per 1k for each result above 10, so a 30-result call costs about $0.03 to $0.06. That roughly reproduces the judge's $0.047 and makes Exa about 20 to 70 times cheaper than Lessie's $1.19 to $1.98. Exa needs no new account, no monthly subscription and no browser OAuth.

On the weak groups, nothing shows Lessie finding picks the incumbents miss. GS-03 Vervloesem and De Cock, GS-22 Danneels, Flaam, Audenaert and Tuyls, and GS-31 Beke are LinkedIn-profile people, and Exa people reaches that data class at a fraction of the cost. GS-08 Joris has an Antwerp base on LinkedIn, so any NY-scoped profile search misses him in either tool. Lessie's one distinct ability is KOL search over Instagram, TikTok and YouTube. That could matter for the creative cases (GS-11 Altenhaus and Vandycke, GS-21 Kegels), but no probe or vendor document shows small Belgian designers in that index. Exa web search already reached Instagram pages in the POC raw recall. A claim I cannot confirm counts as not holding.

The only quality evidence is Lessie's own PeopleSearchBench, which is vendor-authored. The public directory check (0 of 99 gold picks) is uninformative. A pragmatic engineer gives the one LinkedIn benchmark slot to Exa people and drops Lessie.

Two smaller points in the judge note are overstated, though neither saves the rating. First, SKILL.md says B2B mode and enrich_people return "employment history" and "work history", so position dates may exist. Education is still undocumented, so the GS-09 Segers (Vlerick) and GS-01 Vanholder (KU Leuven) ties stay unconfirmed. Second, the 2000-character query can name schools and domains in prose, and review_people accepts checkpoints with category "school". That is soft steering after the search (1 credit and 1 to 3 minutes per person), not a hard filter. Raw copies are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-arend-Developer-FN--claude-worktrees-mvp-tech-research-b285c0/f1ac462c-7dec-4c00-b496-a79f3ccba7cd/scratchpad/rerate/verify-i14/.

rerate.verifier_reason:
The K5 knockout is real under the rules as settled. rerate-and-seeds-plan.md line 24 says a source that needs a personal login or a personal-use licence still fails K5, even though a paid self-serve price on its own no longer does. On 2026-10-29 I fetched belga.press/en/packages/ again (HTTP 200, saved in scratchpad/verify-i15/packages.html). The page says "The app is specifically designed for personal use", allows one device at a time and does not support shared accounts. "Log in" goes to the Keycloak realm at sso.ssl.belga.be (client_id=belgapress-web). The only multi-user option is the tailor-made licence, which says "Contact our specialists", so a sales call is needed and that fails K5 too. The page links no developer, swagger or feed endpoint. The only api.belga.press URL on it is /belgapress/api/public/uploads/packages_hero_image_..., which is a CMS image. Even the self-serve EUR 52.58 + EUR 1.20/article plan is a personal login, so FN cannot query it without automating a personal-use account, and the plan rules that out.

On the weak groups, Belga's full-text archive is the one place that could search topic-first ("Vlaamse ondernemer New York") across the 403 publishers. In principle it could add Dutch tie lines for the unverified picks: Philip Vervloesem (OMP, GS-03), the GS-22 panel (Danneels, Flaam, Audenaert, Tuyls) and D'Hulst (GS-08). It is not reachable, though, so it finds 0 picks in any group. The creative and low-footprint cases (GS-11, GS-12, GS-21, GS-30, GS-24 ocean panel, GS-31 US AI panel) are mostly non-Belgian US people that a Belgian press archive would not surface anyway. The drop survives.

One caveat on the rating's text. The "what_we_take"/"beats_or_loses_to" claim, and the judge note that the web lane's press rows already give the dated Dutch tie line for GS-07, GS-08 and GS-32, are inferred, not shown in the probe. The verdict does not depend on them, because K5 fails on its own. The rating already flags correctly that the earlier reference row's "from EUR 4,250" figure belongs to Belga.share enterprise, not to the archive licence. That row in mvp-tech-reference.md (line 634) should be corrected.

rerate.judge_note: Fails K5. clado.ai returns 503 DEPLOYMENT_PAUSED (I checked probes/i16-home.html), and the YC page redirects to Freesolo, which lists Clado under Previous Launches. The docs name no sign-up, and the newest changelog entry is October 2025, so no key can be bought.
rerate.verifier_reason: The drop stands, but the stated K5 reason is partly wrong, so the ground has to change. I re-probed on 2026-10-29. clado.ai and www.clado.ai/pricing still return 503. docs.clado.ai returns 200, and search.clado.ai/api/search returns 401 without a key. The rater missed one thing: dashboard.clado.ai is live. It is a Next.js "API Dashboard" with Create API Key, Usage, Logs and Billing pages. Its /api/auth/providers lists Google OAuth as the only sign-in, and /login and /billing return 200 (saved as probes/i16v-dashboard.html and probes/i16v-js/). So a self-serve sign-up path exists. I could not confirm that Billing still sells credits without signing in, which the hard rules forbid. Under the rules an unconfirmed claim counts as not holding, so "buyable today" is unproven rather than disproven. The drop holds on two other grounds. First, the vendor is effectively dead: its homepage deployment is paused, YC lists Clado as a previous launch of Freesolo, which now sells post-training tools, and the docs have not changed since October 2025. Building a lane on a product its company has left is a breakage risk with no upside. Second, it duplicates a better live option. Exa already holds FN's key for arm B and documents a people category that returns professional (LinkedIn-derived) profiles. Under the new K6 the re-rating step can turn that on at no extra integration cost. On the weak groups, Clado's LinkedIn records would mainly help business picks: GS-03 (Vervloesem, De Cock), GS-33 (Lemmy, De Cock), GS-22 (Danneels, Flaam, Audenaert) and GS-31 (Jan Beke). Exa's people category reaches those same records. Clado would add little for the creative cases (GS-11 Savonie and Vandycke, GS-12 Kore Yoors, GS-21 Himpe-Depuydt, GS-30 the architects) or for GS-24's ocean scientists, whose evidence sits on event pages and bios, not in profile fields. The rater's gold_cases_helped list also strays outside the weak groups (GS-09, GS-32) and leaves out GS-33 and GS-22. Clado's one edge is structured position dates (date_from_year) for vendor-record claim dates, and the rules already settle that mapping, so there is nothing to borrow.
