Agree: Dellaert (P69 KU Leuven, flemish), Sweldens (KU Leuven), Maes (Vrije Universiteit Brussel), Dewulf (Ghent University), Bruyninckx (KU Leuven), Trouet (KU Leuven), Herdewyn (KU Leuven), Van Hentenryck (University of Namur, belgian), Wilmes (UCLouvain Saint-Louis, belgian), Goemans and de Wit (P27 Belgium only, belgian; Wikidata lacks their UCLouvain/Liege degrees, P69 is only MIT), Steele and Atala (US, none). Also 1 case where Wikidata would say 'none' falsely: Lermusiaux (P69 Harvard only, gold belgian via Liege). Wikidata resolves 1 gold 'unverified': Pim Tuyls Q102293907 'Dr.Sc. KU Leuven 1997' (identity likely, not confirmed). Provenance: of 565 statements on the 15 items, 272 (48%) carry any reference and 58 (10%) carry a P854 URL; on the 50 tie-bearing statements (P27/P69/P108), 34 have a reference and 13 (26%) have P854. Where present the URLs are good (gatech.edu page, ORCID employment API, LinkedIn, arizona.edu faculty page, inspiringfifty.org). Other references use P6634 (LinkedIn id) or P143 (imported from English Wikipedia), which are not URLs. Dates: only 3 of 14 P108 statements have a start date, none has an end date.
probe.notes:
VERDICT: Wikidata is a cheap, free, fast tie-and-identity enrichment step for people already named (about 0.5 s per lookup, no key), not a discovery source and not a source of dated, sourced claims. Use cyanheads (or call the same Wikidata SPARQL/wbsearch endpoints directly) for: P69/P27 tie hints on notable people, ORCID/OpenAlex-to-QID bridging, and Wikipedia sitelinks. Do not build the topic-to-people path on it.

Copy two ideas from the server: orcid_resolve_researcher's candidate ranking by institution overlap, and the affiliation-intersection query, a US employer AND a Flemish university.

name: Web2BigTable: orchestrator plus parallel workers with shared workboard and gap-fill round
what_we_take: The Deep-tier control loop. An orchestrator splits the query into subtasks (sub-topic x institution x source type, e.g. 'Nokia Bell Labs Murray Hill staff with KU Leuven or UGent degrees' for GS-02). Parallel workers each write to one slot on a shared board. A gap round then targets empty rows and missing claims, such as an unsettled tie type. Dedup into F9 runs before results show.
why: It is the only one of the five that answers how to spend an overnight budget so that deeper means more people. The authors report WideSearch success 38.5 vs 5.1 for the next system, but give no cost or latency, so the NFR on recording effort is not met out of the box. The code is a research stack (LangChain orchestrator, FastMCP, Memento-S JSON-ops workers, BM25/bge-m3 skill router, 42 stars). Our own agent loop rebuilds the pattern in less code than adopting theirs, so we copy the design, not the repo.

name: Exa Websets: search, per-criterion verification, enrichment, and a recall estimator
what_we_take: Run Websets with entity=person and three criteria per gold case (topic fit, metro or able to travel, Belgian/Flemish/Dutch education or employer). Each item's evaluations[].references (url, snippet) become claim evidence, and recall=true gives the expected-total estimate. Score the result against the 28 cases.
why: Websets is a credible contender for topic to new people. Each item returns per-criterion reasoning, satisfied yes/no/unclear and references with url and snippet. Person properties include educationHistory, the direct route to tie claims such as KU Leuven for GS-02 or Liège for GS-10. It had the best independent recall of the list-building APIs (19.6% vs FindAll Core 5.5% on NewsCatcher's 32 event queries) and was second in the vendor-run PeopleSearchBench, so it earns a head-to-head run. Three risks the run must show: snippets are nullable (K2 gaps), the person profiles appear LinkedIn-derived (linkedinUrl in work history, a K6 question for Exa's terms), and the dollar price per credit could not be confirmed.

name: Parallel FindAll: match conditions, cited reasoning, generator tiers as a depth ladder
what_we_take: Run FindAll with entity type people. The F1 chips (topic, place, tie) become match_conditions, and each gold case runs at preview, core and pro. Each condition's basis (citations with url and excerpt, reasoning, confidence) is stored as a claim. SSE events stream partial matches to the cards, which tests F7 and the Instant-to-Deep tiering in one run.
why: It maps more directly onto FN's requirements than any other API here. Editable match conditions match the F1 chips, per-field citations with excerpts match K2/F5, SSE and webhooks with partial snapshots match F7, and four priced generator tiers plus extend-runs match F17. Pricing is public: preview $0.10, core $2 + $0.15 per match, pro $10 + $1 per match. A 28-case run at pro with about 20 matches should cost about $840, about $140 at core. The one independent figure is weak (5.5% recall for Core on event queries), it is public beta, and it has no people-search benchmark, so it must earn its place on the gold set.

name: PeopleSearchBench: criteria-grounded verification harness with 28 expert-search queries
what_we_take: The grading step. An LLM splits each gold ask into checkable criteria (topic, metro or able to attend, tie type). Each returned person is checked per criterion against live web results and graded 0/0.5/1 (qualified at 0.5 or above). The Information Utility score (completeness, evidence quality, actionability) is reused to score our cards before a human review of the top 5.
why: FN's precision target needs a human judgement on the top 5 new people for each of 28 cases, about 140 people per option. A criteria-grounded pre-grade reports a kappa of 0.84 against human annotators and lets us triage across Exa, FindAll and our own loop before humans look. We do not adopt the benchmark itself: its 119 queries are recruiting and B2B asks, not FN's gold set, raw results are withheld, and the vendor ranks itself first. The claimed $0.86/query and $150 full-run cost were not in the repo or abstract, so they are dropped.

name: Capture-recapture (Chao) estimator as a stopping rule and coverage estimate
what_we_take: Tag each found person with the discovery paths that found them (web search, OpenAlex topic authors, event or mission programs, Flemish-institution pages, snowball from seeds). After each Deep round, compute f1 (found by one path) and f2 (found by two) and N-hat = n + f1^2/(2 f2). Stop the overnight run when the estimated unfound share stays flat across rounds. The value is recorded with the search's time and cost as a lower-bound coverage figure.
why: The Deep tier needs some rule for when to stop an overnight run, and the NFR needs evidence that deeper means better. This is ten lines of arithmetic over data we already record per search. The evidence is thin for our scale: tested on 94 TAR corpora of 500+ documents, it triggers only after 100+ labels and hit a 95% target in 70% of runs. Our paths share search engines, so f1/f2 will be correlated and N-hat is only a lower bound. We use it as a stop signal and a logged figure, never as a recall claim shown to staff.

facts_checked.claim: Chao 1987 form N = n + f1^2/(2 f2), with f1(f1-1)/(2(f2+1)) when f2 = 0
At a 95% target Chao gave 95.9% recall, 56% WSS and met the target in 70% of runs; AutoStop gave 98.2%, 24% and 89%
Tested on 94 datasets, unstable early
facts_checked.source: Paper: 94 datasets x 30 seeds; criteria trigger after more than 100 labeled documents; datasets under 500 documents excluded

facts_checked.claim: Paper is v1 only, 2024-04-01 preprint (Bron, van der Heijden, Feelders, Siebes)

probe_plan: Keyless probe on GS-02 (6G, NY/NJ) and GS-10 (Belgian faculty at MIT). Path A: OpenAlex /authors filtered by last_known_institutions = Nokia Bell Labs (or MIT), with works on 6G/wireless topics. Path B: Wikidata SPARQL for humans with employer Bell Labs or MIT and educated at a Belgian university (KU Leuven, UGent, UCLouvain, ULiege, ULB). Path C: OpenAlex authors whose affiliation history includes a Belgian institution and now a US one in the metro. Count f1 and f2 across the three paths and compute N-hat. The probe works if Baeyens, Vetter and Sweldens (GS-02) or Goemans, Lermusiaux and de Wit (GS-10) appear in at least two paths and f2 > 0.
beats_or_loses_to: It beats the obvious alternative, stopping on a fixed time or budget, because the stop follows from overlap rather than the clock. It loses to the paper's own AutoStop on reliability, but AutoStop needs a ranked document stream with sampling, which a people search does not produce. It complements Exa's recall flag, a vendor estimate we cannot inspect, and gives an independent number for the head-to-head.
pricing_terms: Method only, no license issue.
what_it_is: Technology-assisted-review stopping method. Several independent discovery methods each 'capture' relevant items. Items found by exactly 1 and exactly 2 methods (f1, f2) give an estimate of how many remain unfound (N = n + f1^2 / 2 f2 style). Worked example: found 92, estimate 116.2, truth 120.

name: REFLECT: LLM judges are unreliable at evidence verification
requirements_served: NFR Explainability (100% of claims have URL, quote, date)
POC lesson: every AI step checked against the gold set
what_we_take: One rule for our claim verifier and our eval harness: a claim counts as supported only if its quote appears verbatim (after whitespace and case normalization) in the stored page text and the page date parses, and any LLM judge we keep scores one claim at a time, never a whole card or report.
why: Table 1 of the paper shows the best judge below 55% overall, 51.9% on tool-use groundedness (Claude-Opus-4.7) and 38.0% on reasoning faithfulness. Wrong Source Citation and Evidence Fabrication are exactly the failures FN must not show on a card. The same paper reports up to about 30 points gained from fine-grained over holistic judging, which is why per-claim judging is part of the rule; the rest is a string check that costs nothing, so this is a few hours of work and needs no dependency.

facts_checked.claim: arXiv 2605.19196 exists, submitted 2026-05-18, v1 only
Best judge below 55% overall; evidence verification weakest
Taxonomy includes Wrong Source Citation, Evidence Fabrication, Citation Groundedness
Fine-grained judging gains up to about 30 points over holistic
Code or dataset released

name: Exa people-search evaluation design (targeted lookup recall@k plus role-based LLM-judged discovery)
requirements_served: Differentiator: recall and reach into people with little web footprint
NFR Effort and quality (deeper must score higher)
POC lesson: every AI step checked against the gold set on each change
what_we_take: The hold-out lookup test: take people from the imported Excel list (F15) who have a public page, generate a query from their topic, institution and place without their name, and score recall@1 and recall@10 per depth. The query generation and recall scoring in exa-labs/benchmarks (MIT, data/people.jsonl) are the template.
why: The gold set has 28 cases and 63 picks. Hold-out queries from the existing list give hundreds more labelled cases at no labelling cost, so we can check on every change that Deep beats Quick on recall. The dataset and harness exist (exa-labs/benchmarks, 40 commits, 16 stars, MIT). We drop its 1,400 role-based US queries ('mid-level onboarding specialists in San Diego') because they do not look like FN asks, and its reported scores (Exa R@10 94.5%, Brave 77.9%, Parallel 74.7%) are vendor-run with older adapters. For the discovery half, we copy the judge that fetches each result's page only under the REFLECT rule: a verbatim quote check, then one LLM call per claim.

name: Parallel Task API 'Basis' (field-level evidence)
what_we_take: For each candidate we run one Task API call with a claims output schema (topic, tie_type, availability, location, role) and store each basis entry (citation url + excerpts, confidence) as the claim. Low confidence, null excerpts or no citation is shown as 'missing'. The source date comes from our own fetch.
why: This is the per-person verification step. It works on names from any discovery source (Websets, FindAll, FRIS, OpenAlex, the network sheet), and it gives the source URL and excerpt per field that F5 needs. Building that ourselves means a search, fetch and LLM-extract loop, which is the same Tavily plus Gemini pipeline that silently broke verification in the POC. Pricing is public and fits the depth ladder: Lite $5 per 1,000 runs (5 to 60 s) for Quick, Core $25 (1 to 5 min) for Extended, Ultra $300 (5 to 25 min) for Deep. That is $0.005 to $0.30 per person, and 5,000 free requests a month covers every gold-set run. Its siblings are Websets evaluations, which only cover people Websets found itself, and FindAll, which does discovery; neither verifies a name handed in from elsewhere, so this does not double up a sibling.

what_we_take: We use the public PersonServiceFRIS SOAP getPersons call (no key) as the name-to-Flemish-affiliation check. It returns the current institution and unit, ORCID, research expertise text and a lastModified date, which become a Flemish tie claim and a role claim with a quote and date for Flanders-based candidates. It also gives FRIS uuid/ORCID as identifiers for F9 dedup.
why: I ran it live on 2026-10-28 and it found 7 of 8 gold-set picks tested. Hans Bruyninckx (GS-28) came back at UAntwerpen Politics & Public Governance with expertise text 'European Environment and climate policies, Global environmental governance', modified 2026-10-28. The others were Leen Govaerts at VITO (C-02), Peter Lievens, Bieke Zaman and Gert-Jan Put (C-03), Daan van Heesch at KU Leuven Art History (GS-16) and Valerie Trouet with an FWO record linked to University of Arizona (GS-28). Yves Baeyens, who is US-based, was correctly absent. That is the 18-of-63 'flown in from Belgium' group that US web search misses, under a free license. Use is limited by what failed. probe.notes:
STATUS (checked 2026-10-28): alive. Endpoint https://frisr4.researchportal.be/ws/PersonService (also ProjectService, OrganisationService; WSDL at ?wsdl) returns CERIF 1.5 XML dated 2026-10-28, so data is current. SOAP only, no key, no JSON. Terms and licence NOT verified: https://www.researchportal.be/en/ returned HTTP 403 to plain curl; a retry with a browser User-Agent was blocked as bot-check circumvention and I stopped; the web-search budget was also spent. K6 stays open for FRIS. OpenAlex: one keyless call on 2026-10-28 returned Rate limit exceeded: no API key, free daily budget shared by IP, 0 remaining, resets midnight UTC. So the OpenAlex hit-count comparison was not run, and I did not create a key (hard rule). Treat openalex works keyless as stale; a free key is now needed.

API SHAPE (differs from rater plan): window needs pageSize <= 100 plus an orderings element with a real id (person.name, locale en_GB, direction ASCENDING or DESCENDING; ASC is rejected). pageSize 200 gives a bare 500 fault, so the earlier pageSize 200 run must have fallen back to the default 10-row window. Working request body: personCriteria containing window(pageSize 100, pageNumber 0, orderings/order(id person.name, locale en_GB, direction ASCENDING)) then name/search SURNAME; SOAPAction empty.

NAME SEARCH IS WEAK. Multi-word search is OR: Martens Luc returned 9,144 rows; quoted phrase, AND and plus-prefixed variants returned 9,144 to 9,936 rows. Only the surname is usable and first name must be filtered client-side. Rare surnames work (Ertas 3 rows, Herdewyn 16, Sweldens 18, Trogh 23, Depreeuw 27). Common ones do not: Claeys 1,313 rows, Martens 2,350 rows, with unreliable ordering; Claeys page 6 and Martens page 10 held no Manu Claeys or Luc Martens. Luc M. Martens is a UGent professor so he is very likely in FRIS; the miss is the search, not the data. The same person appears once per provider institution (Ertas: KU Leuven, UHasselt, VUB rows; only the KU Leuven row has ORCID 0009-0009-3086-0259 and assignments), so dedup needs ORCID or cross-provider IDs. Peter Vetter returns 106 rows including 10 Peter Vetter UGent rows: ambiguous. Many rows have only name and provider ID (Trogh, Dellaert).

TOPIC SEARCH DOES NOT RETURN PEOPLE. PersonService keyword criterion returned a 500 fault (with and without locale); its generic search only matches names (offshore wind returned people surnamed Wind). ProjectService name search works: offshore wind gave 86 projects (10 on the default page) with title, abstract, keywords, start date, funding, sometimes an org unit, e.g. Circular transition in offshore wind (CTO), start 2022-01-01. The project rows I inspected had no person links (cfProj_Pers count 0). ProjectService keyword gave a 500 fault. Not tested: publications, per-person project joins via associatedPersons.

PRAGMATIC RATING: use as a Flemish tie checker (K3; supports F5/F6 dated claims), not a discovery engine. Given a candidate name from web search, one surname query (about 0.25 s) returns ORCID, institution IDs and dated KU Leuven/UGent/VUB/UAntwerp memberships, which targets the gap that 36 of 99 gold people have an unsettled tie. Public government endpoint, fits the seconds depth tier. Cost: small SOAP/XML client (about 100 lines) plus a rule that shows a tie only with ORCID or exact first name plus affiliation overlap, else label it possible. It cannot find overseas people with a Flemish tie unless they hold a record, cannot answer who-knows-X, and is useless for non-academics (Claeys, Desruelle, Vervloesem, entrepreneurs). Projects by topic can name Flemish orgs but not people.

NEW PLAUSIBLE PEOPLE: none; results were name homonyms, not topical candidates.

name: PeopleSearchBench (criteria-grounded verification benchmark)
what_we_take: We copy the scoring step. Each gold-set ask is split into checkable criteria (topic, place, tie type, ask), every returned new person is auto-checked per criterion with a live search, and the fraction of criteria met is reported. That pre-screens precision for every option, and a human then reviews only the top 5 per case.
why: Our gold set measures recall with known picks, but precision needs a human pass on 28 cases x 5 people x every option. The paper reports kappa 0.84 between its automatic verifier and human annotators, which means the auto-check can rank options before the human pass. We do not adopt the repo. It has 6 commits, no releases, raw per-person results withheld, and it is tied to Tavily plus an unnamed OpenRouter judge. The scoring is roughly a day to rebuild on top of the Parallel Task call we adopt anyway. The authors rank their own product first, so their system ranking is ignored.

name: OpenAlex as the topic-to-people graph: topic hierarchy, author topics, dated affiliations, authorship countries
what_we_take: The authors endpoint as a keyless candidate generator and tie-evidence source: filter topics.id + last_known_institutions (or country) + affiliations.institution.country_code:BE, then cite the specific work's authorship (institution, year, URL) as the dated Belgian/Flemish tie claim.
why: I probed it live without a key. MIT authors with any BE affiliation returned 318 people, including 3 of the 4 GS-10 MIT academics (Goemans, Lermusiaux, de Wit; Janjevic missing) plus Flemish faculty such as Pattie Maes. Wind-energy topic + US base + BE affiliation returned 14 candidates, and Yves Baeyens (GS-02) carries IMEC (BE) 1996-2002, which is a dated Flemish-institution tie. Precision needs a ranking step, because CERN/CMS collaboration papers flood the BE filter and a naive 'BE before US' rule dropped Goemans and Lermusiaux. Siblings are useless for topic expansion: 'Wind Energy' has 'Antenna Design' as a sibling. Profiles are overmerged (Baeyens shows a hospital and Parma) and his last_known_institutions is empty, so a claim must cite the work, not the profile. OpenAlex is the only free source that ties topic, affiliation country and year together; ORCID covers about 1 in 10 authors and lacks topics.

name: Balog language-model framework: profile-centric (Model 1) vs document-centric (Model 2) expert finding
what_we_take: Model 2B scoring for web discovery: rank pages for the topic, link a person to a page only through a text window around the name (that window becomes the claim quote), and sum page scores per person so that someone on four relevant pages outranks someone on one. For instant network search, a Model 1 per-person profile in a lexical+vector index, with no LLM rerank in the hot path.
why: The paper confirms it. Model 2 beat Model 1 on TREC 2006 (MAP .4660 vs .3206, MRR .9354 vs .7264, significant), and window-based 1B gave up to 32% MAP over Model 1. The aggregation rule is a concrete answer to how F4 ranks new people from many pages, and the window ties ranking to the K2 quote. It assumes a known candidate list on an intranet, so open-web enumeration and dedup stay ours. The numbers are 2005-2006 intranet results, so they are only a direction.

facts_checked.claim: Balog, Azzopardi, de Rijke, 'A language modeling framework for expert finding', IP&M (accepted June 2008)

what_it_is: Classic TREC Enterprise generative models. Model 1 builds a text profile per candidate from associated documents and scores it against the topic. Model 2 ranks documents for the topic, then adds up the evidence of candidates associated with each. Variants 1B/2B use only text in a window around the name.

name: WideSearch: benchmark and metrics for 'find all, then fill the table' agents
what_we_take: Two scores per run on the 28 gold cases. Item-level: the share of known picks found. Row-level: picks found with the correct tie type and a dated, sourced claim. Each miss gets a label from WideSearch's error taxonomy (incomplete query decomposition, no reflection or refinement, failed evidence use, hallucination).
why: The gold set already holds a tie label per person, so the Item vs Row split is computable today and shows whether deeper runs fix claims or only add names. Multi-agent runs beat single-agent runs on the same model (o3 Row F1 34.0 to 37.8; Sonnet 4 31.7 to 38.5). That backs parallel fan-out, which the POC lessons already require, so it adds evidence and no new decision. The tasks and code (MIT, ByteDance Seed) are Chinese and English table tasks, and running them would test generic agents, not FN.

name: Ko-WideSearch: finding the set is easy, filling each row is the bottleneck
what_we_take: Split the pipeline in two. Stage 1 enumerates candidate names. Stage 2 runs a separate, targeted search and page read per person for each free-text claim (tie, ability to attend). Extended and Deep spend most of their budget on stage 2 with new source types, not on more stage-1 queries. An unfilled cell shows as 'not found'.
why: Across 20 agents, Item-F1 was 92.8 against Row-F1 53.7. More search or spend did not close the gap, and free-text cells failed most. FN's tie and availability claims are exactly those free-text cells, and prior work could not settle the tie for 36 of 99 people. So 'deeper means better' (F17) has to come from per-person claim work, and the progressive cards (F7) fall out of the split. WideSearch already supplies the metric, so this entry contributes only the architecture rule. The paper is a single-author v1 on Korean tasks with no code, so it supports a design rule, not a number to plan on.

why: Its set F1 and 'fully correct' scores need a closed answer set. name: Folded name key plus identifier-first rule (stdlib only)
requirements_served: Duplicates: shared identifier means same person
Duplicates: same person never twice in one result list

what_we_take: Tier 1 exact match on normalized identifiers (profile URL, website, ORCID, OpenAlex, Wikidata, email), then a per-field folded key (surname key and given-name key stored as columns on Person) used to block candidates, with tier 3 nicknames plus one shared fact raising a pair only to 'flag'.
why: This is the cheapest way to meet the written duplicate rules, and it implements the doc's own tiers. I ran it and found 2 defects to fix before adoption. First, the key is order-dependent on the full name ('Peeters, Jan' gives peetersjan, 'Jan Peeters' gives janpeeters), so the key must be computed per field (surname, given) and not on the full string. Second, the ASCII-only regex silently drops letters ('Søren Ødegård' gives srendegard, 'Łukasz' gives ukasz), so use a Unicode \W strip or anyascii (ISC, 0.3.3). Blocking cost is also smaller than claimed: F9 compares about 50 candidates per search against 10,000 rows, and only the one-time F15 import needs the self-join, which surname-key blocking makes trivial.

why: The toolkit itself is shaped for OpenReview. Its examples fetch data with OpenReview credentials and expect a per-reviewer jsonl archive format, so the 20 to 30 lines of logic we need are cheaper to copy than to wrap. The recipe fits FN well: max-aggregation returns one concrete paper, which gives F5 a URL, a quote and a date, and the recency filter covers the 'base and role go stale' lesson. The gold-standard study (58 researchers, 477 scores) shows SPECTER2 best on titles and abstracts, misranking 12-30% of easy and 36-43% of hard pairs, with off-the-shelf LLMs behind, so we use it as a cheap pre-ranker before the LLM claim check, never as the final judge.

name: LLMScholarBench: LLMs recommending experts from memory, and what web RAG changes
what_we_take: Two eval-harness items. Run each gold case several times and report the consistency of the names returned next to recall, and pin temperature low for the name-enumeration step.
why: The main lesson, never trust model memory for names, is already settled by K2 and F6 and needs no new source. FN's 100% sourced-claim rule already covers the factuality metric, so it adds nothing. What is new and concrete is the finding that higher temperature lowers validity, consistency and factuality, and that interventions trade metrics rather than all improving. Our discovery step is nondeterministic, so a recall from one run per case is noise, and repeat-run consistency is a cheap check with no human. The diversity and parity findings are physics-specific and need a hypothetical to matter here, so we drop them.

name: Biased assessment of expert-finding benchmarks (annotations validated by the system under test)
what_we_take: A synonym-rewrite variant of the 28 gold asks (for example 'next-generation wireless' for '6G', 'ocean policy' for 'ocean governance'), scored next to the original wording, so options that only match literal terms are exposed before we choose.

It does apply to the planned human precision review: reviewers who label only what an option suggests are judging system-proposed candidates, and the paper shows that this inflates term-based methods. The synonym test is a concrete, cheap fix: 28 rewritten asks, no new labels. My own OpenAlex probe already showed recall swinging with query wording ('6G radio sub-THz' vs 'sub-terahertz wireless transceiver').

name: Anthropic Citations API (document blocks)
requirements_served: NFR explainability (100% of claims with URL, quote, date)
what_we_take: Per fetched page, one Claude Haiku 5.5 call with the trafilatura text (or the raw PDF for mission programs) as a citations-enabled document block; every claim line (topic fit, tie type, ability to attend) must carry a char_location or page_location citation, and a claim without one is stored and shown as missing.
why: It is the only option in this batch where the API itself extracts cited_text from our document, and the docs say citations are 'guaranteed to contain valid pointers to the provided documents'. For GS-02 the Bell Labs bio sentence 'MSc 1992 and PhD 1997 KU Leuven' becomes the Flemish-tie quote for Yves Baeyens, and for GS-04 the 'PhD University of Namur' sentence lets staff check Belgian versus Flemish for Van Hentenryck. Cost is about $0.0005 of input for a 5k-token page at $0.10/MTok, cited_text is not billed as output, and the Batch API halves overnight runs. The known limits hold: it returns a 400 when combined with output_config.format, so we keep structure in text-block prefixes ('TIE: flemish ...') rather than a JSON schema; scanned PDFs cannot be cited; and a pointer does not prove the quote supports the claim, which the gold-set review has to measure.

name: Google LangExtract (source-grounding and alignment algorithm)
what_we_take: The AlignmentStatus idea (match_exact, match_lesser, match_fuzzy, None): an exact, whitespace-normalized substring check of each quote against our stored trafilatura text, with an LCS fallback at 0.75 token coverage, applied only to quotes that do not come from the Citations API (for example excerpts returned by a hosted deep-research or search API under benchmark); a quote that cannot be aligned is shown as missing.
why: For our own extraction the Citations API already guarantees pointers, so the library itself would be a second extractor doing the same job, and Claude is not built in: the only Anthropic route is the community LiteLLM provider or langextract-claude 0.1.0 from 2026-03-05, which has had no release since. The real gap is quotes from third parties. Any discovery API we benchmark returns its own excerpts, and the NFR says every shown quote must be checkable against the stored page. resolver.py runs to 1,443 lines, so we copy the status enum and the exact-then-fuzzy order in about 50 lines, not the whole module.

why: It covers the grounding check, the retry and the streaming card in one dependency, and it has the agent loop the Extended and overnight depths need. Instructor covers only the first of those. The obvious alternative is Claude's Citations API, which returns exact cited_text with char offsets at no output-token cost. The docs say it returns a 400 error when combined with structured outputs, and it attaches citations to text blocks, not typed claims, so it would need a second parse step. Two details to build in: validators also run on every partial snapshot, so skip the check while ctx.partial_output is True, and set retries={'output': 2} or more because the default is 1.

name: normalize-url (and w3lib canonicalize_url) for profile URLs
requirements_served: Duplicates: records that share an identifier (profile URL, website) are the same person

why: Tier 1 is only as good as URL equality. For example, linkedin.com/in/x and www.linkedin.com/in/x/?utm_source=... must match for the import and for F9. Hand-rolled URL() cleanup is the obvious alternative, but it misses default ports, IDN hosts and duplicate slashes, which this library already handles. normalize-url 10.0.0 was published to npm on 2026-10-14 under MIT. It is ESM-only (package type 'module'). Adopt at most one of the two: w3lib canonicalize_url is a crawler canonicaliser, and I did not confirm that it strips www or utm params by default. Pick w3lib 2.5.0 (PyPI, 2026-09-30) only if the stack turns out to be Python, and then add those two rules by hand.

name: OpenRefine clustering (human pass on the one-time import)
what_we_take: Copy the fingerprint key-collision method as the tier 2 blocking key: trim, lowercase, ASCII-fold, drop punctuation, split into tokens, dedupe and sort. That makes 'Peeters, Jan' and 'Jan Peeters' collide. Our own rules then add the Van de/Vande join and the nickname table.
why: Running OpenRefine itself would give import dedup a second owner: staff would clean the sheet with OpenRefine's rules before import, and FN's own flag rules would run again afterwards. Importing every row through FN's F9 matcher and resolving flags in the F11 Merge / Keep separate screen keeps one owner. It also tests that screen on real data before any web search runs. The keying algorithm is the reusable part. It is about 15 lines and works on the full 10,000-row list in the app's language. The latest release is 3.10.1 ('04 Mar', no year shown). I could not confirm the licence because the GitHub API was rate-limited, but a borrowed algorithm does not depend on it.

name: Wayback Machine CDX server (first-capture date)

name: Anthropic web_search server tool
what_we_take: Nothing as the search backend. If the agent runs on Claude, keep the documented max_uses guidance (1-3 searches for a simple query, 10+ for multi-entity) as a starting depth dial for a client-side search tool.

name: Reciprocal rank fusion to merge candidate lists from many query expansions and sources
what_we_take: Score = sum of 1/(k + rank) over every list a person appears in (k=60), used to merge the network lexical and vector lists for Instant search, and to merge the per-expansion and per-source candidate lists (web, OpenAlex, Wikidata, network) at Quick and deeper.
why: It needs no training data, which FN lacks with 28 gold cases. It takes about 10 lines and runs in microseconds, so Instant search can drop the LLM rerank that made the POC take 16 to 27 s and return everyone when the rerank failed. It rewards people found by several sub-queries, such as a Bell Labs fellow who shows up under both '6G' and 'RF integrated circuits'. Both obvious alternatives lose: CombSUM/CombMNZ need calibrated scores that web search and OpenAlex do not share, and a learned fuser needs labels we do not have.

facts_checked.claim: Elasticsearch ships RRF as a generally available retriever, with rank_constant defaulting to 60 and the 1/(k+rank) formula
Qdrant supports RRF and DBSF fusion and calls RRF the safe default when there is no eval set; its default k is 2, not 60
RRF is the default hybrid method in every hybrid-search stack
facts_checked.source: Elastic docs do not call it the default. Qdrant offers it next to DBSF and weighted RRF.

facts_checked.claim: The SIGIR 2009 paper found that k=60 is near-optimal but not critical

beats_or_loses_to: Wins over CombMNZ and score normalisation, because web-search ranks, OpenAlex relevance and vector cosine are on different scales. Wins over keeping the POC LLM rerank in Instant search, because of latency and the failure mode. Pairs with the RankGPT finding (RRF narrows to the top 50, then an LLM orders those), so they do not compete. If a store with built-in RRF gets picked (Elastic, Qdrant), use its built-in version and pass k=60 explicitly, since Qdrant's default is 2.
cost_note: Free; no dependency needed.
pricing_terms: None.
what_it_is: Score = sum over lists of 1/(k + rank), k=60. Merges rankings from different systems without training. In the paper it beat Condorcet Fuse and CombMNZ and individual learning-to-rank methods on TREC runs and LETOR 3.

name: LLM query expansion: gains and the failure on unfamiliar or ambiguous queries
what_we_take: Two rules for the F1 parser: (1) ground sub-topics in OpenAlex topic names and in retrieved pages, rather than taking only the LLM's own pseudo-document, and show them as deletable chips; (2) when the topic is niche or ambiguous (e.g. 'Jan Yoors', 'Flemish prints'), skip LLM expansion or take sub-topics only from pages already retrieved.
why: Expansion is needed. In a live OpenAlex probe, the GS-02 pick Yves Baeyens has no last-known institution, so the query '6G' filtered to Nokia (US) did not return him, nor Vetter or Klein. His OpenAlex topics are 'Radio Frequency Integrated Circuit Design' and 'Advanced Photonic Communication Systems', which a grounded expansion would match. The SIGIR 2025 paper names the failure that bites FN's long tail (GS-12 Jan Yoors, GS-16 Netherlandish prints, GS-13 Antwerp Ring): the LLM's gap in knowledge, not hallucination, makes the expansions wrong or too narrow. Query2doc as a method adds nothing beyond 'the LLM writes sub-queries', which any agent does already, so we take the guard rules and not a library.

name: Wikidata SPARQL for tie-seeded people lists (educated at Flemish universities)
what_we_take: A tie-claim lookup: for a candidate with a Wikidata QID, read educated at (P69), employer (P108), citizenship (P27) and birthplace (P19), then type the tie from a small table of university QIDs (Flemish: KU Leuven Q833670, UGent Q1137665, VUB Q612665, UAntwerp; Belgian francophone: UCLouvain, Liège, Namur, ULB; Dutch universities). The claim cites the item URL, the statement's reference URL when there is one, and the read date. The QID also serves as an identifier for dedup.
why: A live probe found 5 Flemish-tie gold picks with the education that decides the tie: Dellaert (KU Leuven, Georgia Tech), Trouet (KU Leuven, U Arizona), Sweldens (KU Leuven), Maes (VUB, MIT) and Dewulf (Ghent, Berkeley). It also gave Van Hentenryck as Namur-educated, which yields the Belgian-not-Flemish label the gold set records. That is the exact tie typing F4 asks for, at zero cost, under CC0. The tie-seeded people list itself is weak for discovery. KU Leuven 214, Ghent 183 and VUB 59 alumni have a US employer, but only 64 of those 456 carry a field of work, so topic fit must come from elsewhere. name: RankGPT-style listwise LLM reranking of candidate evidence cards
what_we_take: The listwise prompt: give the LLM the top 20-50 fused candidates as short claim cards with ids and ask for a full permutation plus a one-line reason that cites card claim ids. On failure, keep the RRF order and cut to the top N. Skip the sliding window, because 50 cards fit one context.
why: The target is 3 of the top 5 new people judged good, and that order depends on judgement across candidates (topic fit, tie type, ability to attend), which RRF alone cannot weigh. The listwise prompt is the useful part. The 2023 paper's sliding window (window 20, step 10 over 100 passages) solved context limits that current models no longer hit at 50 cards, and its distillation result concerns a ranker FN will not train. So the paper adds a prompt pattern, not code; the Apache-2.0 repo shows 666 stars and no releases, and FN does not need it.

what_we_take: The pair review queue: two records side by side, a per-field choice of surviving value, and 'Merge and review next' / 'Keep separate and review next' buttons that move to the next flagged pair. why: This is the queue F15 needs for the one-time Excel import, where hundreds of pairs get reviewed in one sitting, and the same queue serves the duplicate card in F9. name: yente logic-v2 (explained score pattern)
requirements_served: Duplicates: name variant plus one shared fact
what_we_take: Two things. First, a plain-language reason on each duplicate flag ('Possibly Jan Peeters: same surname, given name is a known variant, same employer'). Second, a fixed points-off rule when a fact conflicts. Logic-v2 takes 0.20 off for a country mismatch and 0.15 or 0.25 for a birth-date mismatch. FN would take points off for a different employer or a different city.
why: The MVP doc flags a duplicate on a name variant plus one shared fact (employer, city or a source). A reason sentence on the card lets staff check that fact without opening both records. The matcher page confirms the penalties: -0.20 for different countries, -0.15 for birth year, -0.25 for birth day, -0.20 for gender. Do not adopt yente, which needs Elasticsearch or OpenSearch. Do not adopt nomenklatura either: it holds the logic-v2 code (4.17.5, MIT, released 2026-10-27) and runs without Elasticsearch, but it pulls in followthemoney and a pinned scikit-learn, and its rules are tuned for sanctions screening, with no employer or city rule.

name: rigour (OpenSanctions name library)
what_we_take: Two comparison rules. Given names compare only with given names and family names only with family names, and an initial can match a full middle name. A split or join of separators costs little ('cost_sep_drop'), so 'Vanholder' matches 'Van Holder' and 'De Cock' matches 'DeCock'. Accent folding (Stephanie vs Stéphanie) comes from the stdlib.
why: Gold-set names carry Flemish particles and accents (Paul De Cock, Han Vanholder, Bram Vandenbroucke, Stéphanie Rutten). A naive split or a raw string match fails on exactly these, and the POC's name-only dedup already missed pairs. We do not take rigour as a dependency. Its docs have no worked example for person matching, it has no nickname data (OpenSanctions says alias dictionaries are not included), and the F9 rule needs only about 30 lines of normalisation on top of a variant table.

name: Cited but Not Verified (source attribution in deep research agents)
what_we_take: Its three citation checks as FN's per-claim gate and gold-set metric: the URL resolves (validity), the quote is found verbatim in the stored page text (deterministic), and an LLM judge confirms the quote supports the claim (factual accuracy); the score is reported per depth.
why: The paper (arXiv 2605.06635, 2026-05-07) finds frontier models keep link validity above 94% and relevance above 80%, but citation factual accuracy is only 39-77%. Accuracy also drops about 42% as tool calls scale from 2 to 150. That matches the POC lesson that one schema detail broke verification for months unnoticed. FN's 'the sourced claim is the check' design only holds if the quote is shown to support the claim, and the paper also shows deeper is not automatically better, which the 'deeper must mean better' NFR has to measure rather than assume. No code or dataset is released, so we copy the method, not a tool.

what_we_take: The gate design: after the substring check, split each claim into one atomic sentence, score it supported or unsupported against each chunk of the source, keep the max score, and drop or mark missing (F6) any claim below the threshold. Run it as a Claude Haiku yes/no call, not with the MiniCheck model.
why: Substring verification alone lets a real quote back the wrong claim. Example: a quote 'joined Alcatel in Antwerp' does not support 'studied at KU Leuven', and the 'unverified' tie cases in GS-03 show where the tie label goes wrong. The model itself is the wrong pick for the MVP. Its newest dated update is Sept 2024, Dutch is not stated anywhere, the 7B model needs a licensing contact with Bespoke Labs, and FN already calls an LLM, so one Haiku call per claim adds no new runtime. Cost and latency are uncapped in the MVP, so MiniCheck's cost advantage pays nothing back.

name: OpenAI web search and Gemini Google Search grounding citations
what_we_take: Nothing. Anthropic web search already returns `cited_text` (up to 150 chars from the source) and `page_age` for each result. Anthropic web fetch with citations enabled returns `cited_text`, `char_location` and `retrieved_at`, so the URL, quote and date FN needs come from one API.
why: Both return url_citation spans that point into the generated answer, with no quote from the source and no page date, so they fail K2 unless we fetch and verify every page ourselves. Gemini's terms also require showing up to 5 Search Suggestions with each grounded result, cap stored grounded text at two years, and forbid building an index from returned links. That conflicts with FN keeping Source records and reusing tie claims across searches. The Anthropic tools cost $10 per 1,000 searches (fetch adds only tokens) and leave none of these gaps, so there is no second provider to keep.

name: SQLite FTS5 (bm25, trigram, prefix, snippet)
what_we_take: One FTS5 table over person name, role, employer, institutions and claim quotes with column-weighted bm25() and prefix='2 3', plus a second trigram table on names for substring dedup candidates, with snippet() supplying the matched quote.
why: It ships inside SQLite, so the lexical leg costs no new dependency, no service and no index-sync code beyond triggers. At 10,000 rows it answers in milliseconds, so the POC's 16 to 27 s comes from the rerank, not from search. Two corrections: trigram does exact substring matching only, not misspelling tolerance. It catches 'Niko' in 'Nikolai' but not 'Bill'/'William', and it never matches queries shorter than 3 characters, so F9 still needs the shared-fact rule. Lexical search alone misses 'offshore wind' against a claim about 'turbine foundations', so it needs the vector leg in the next finding. DuckDB FTS loses because it does not update on insert.

Prefix index syntax prefix='2 3'
snippet() returns matched text with markers, up to 64 tokens
Trigram tokenizer catches misspelled names
facts_checked.source: https://www.sqlite.org/fts5.html: trigram matches substrings only; substrings under 3 chars match nothing

facts_checked.claim: Public domain, bundled with SQLite

beats_or_loses_to: Beats DuckDB FTS (no incremental update) and a hosted Typesense/Meilisearch (extra service against K5 for 10k rows). It does not compete with sqlite-vec: the two are the two legs of the same fused query.
pricing_terms: Free, public domain
what_it_is: SQLite's built-in full-text engine. It has bm25() with per-column weights, a trigram tokenizer for substring and misspelled-name matching, prefix indexes for type-ahead, and snippet()/highlight() for the matched quote.

name: sqlite-vec + FTS5 reciprocal rank fusion (Alex Garcia hybrid pattern)
what_we_take: The single-SQL RRF query (two CTEs ranked with row_number(), full outer join, score = w/(60+rank) per leg, missing leg counts 0) as the instant network ranker with no LLM in the p50 path, using a vec0 table of claim or person embeddings.
why: RRF always returns a bounded top-k, so it cannot fail open like the POC rerank that returned everyone. Brute-force KNN over 10k vectors costs a few ms. sqlite-vec v0.1.9 (31 Mar 2026) is the latest stable release, and 0.1.10 is alpha. Pin 0.1.9; ANN indexes are not needed at this size. Location should not go into the KNN as a metro_id filter. Arend's 2026-10-28 update makes location one factor, not a filter, so add it as a third RRF term (a distance rank from GeoNames coordinates). vec0 metadata has no IS NULL, so store availability 'unknown' as a string. The F12 list-page filters are plain SQL and do not need vec0.

facts_checked.claim: Latest stable v0.1.9 on 31 Mar 2026; v0.1.10 alphas to 18 May add DiskANN/IVF/rescore
RRF k=60, weights per leg, full outer join
vec0 metadata columns support =, !=, <, <=, >, >= inside KNN; no IS NULL/LIKE; max 16 metadata, 4 partition keys
100k x 1024-dim brute force under 75 ms on M1 mini
facts_checked.source: 2024 stable-release benchmark post as reported; 10k figure is extrapolation, not re-measured

facts_checked.claim: MIT/Apache-2.0 dual license

beats_or_loses_to: Beats the POC's lexical+vector+LLM rerank, which took 16-27 s and failed open. It ties with storing vectors as BLOBs and computing cosine in numpy, which is about as fast at 10k rows; sqlite-vec wins only because the fusion stays in one SQL query and one file. Pairs with FTS5 rather than replacing it. The embedding model is a separate choice and not part of this finding.
pricing_terms: MIT and Apache-2.0
what_it_is: A single SQL query that runs an FTS5 MATCH and a vec0 KNN query, then fuses ranks with score = w_fts/(60+rank_fts) + w_vec/(60+rank_vec) using a full outer join. sqlite-vec is the author's pure-C vector extension for SQLite. vec0 has metadata columns (=, !=, <, > filters inside KNN) and partition keys.

name: Claude Haiku 5.5 with structured outputs for query-to-chips (F1)
requirements_served: NFR every AI step checked against gold set
what_we_take: One Haiku 5.5 call with output_config.format json_schema returns {topics[], institutions[], place_text, ask enum, quote spans}, the code checks each span against the query text, and the chip strings are resolved against the local ROR and GeoNames tables.
why: Constrained decoding is GA on claude-haiku-5-5, which is the fastest and cheapest current model (from $0.10/$0.50 per MTok). A 400-token parse therefore costs a small fraction of a cent, and the schema-drift bug that broke POC verification for months cannot recur silently. Three corrections to the finding: enums may hold numbers, booleans or null, simple regex patterns are supported, and enum casing is not guaranteed, so compare enums case-insensitively. Latency is not measured, so run the FTS leg on the raw query text in parallel with the parse and re-rank when the chips arrive. That keeps the instant p50 under 2 s even if the parse takes over 1 s.

name: Typesense v30.x (geo filter + hybrid + NL search in one binary)
what_we_take: The geo sort with exclude_radius and precision buckets: everyone inside the radius ties on distance and topic fit decides, while people outside sort in 'precision'-mile buckets. Rebuild it as a bucketed distance term in our own ranking SQL.
why: This rule is what 'location is one factor, not a filter' means in practice. Inside the radius, an expert in Murray Hill and one in Manhattan rank on topic, and someone flown in from Belgium only drops a bucket. The server itself adds a second store that must be kept in sync with the person/claim/decision model on every Add, Merge (F11) and edit, and for 10k rows SQLite FTS5 plus vectors plus haversine already covers F3/F8/F12. Its docs show geo filters only on keyword search, not inside vector or hybrid queries, which is the combination FN would need.

name: Postgres stack: pgvector + pg_trgm (+ ParadeDB pg_search)
what_we_take: One Postgres holds the data model (person, source, claim, search, decision) and runs F3 as tsvector full-text plus pgvector cosine, merged with RRF in one SQL query, plus pg_trgm (with unaccent) to flag duplicate candidates for F9/F15; we skip ParadeDB.
why: FN needs a relational store anyway for claims, sources, decisions, atomic Add and Merge-with-both-sources (F10, F11), so search in the same database means no second index to keep in sync. At 10k rows an exact vector scan plus tsvector answers well under the 2 s p50 with no LLM in the instant path, which fixes the POC's 16-27 s and its 'returned everyone' failure. ParadeDB's AGPL BM25 adds little over tsvector at 10k short bios, so we leave it out; pg_trgm scores 'Niko Peeters' vs 'Nikolai Peeters' at 0.71 but 'Bob Smith' vs 'Robert Smith' at only 0.35, so we still need a small nickname table plus the 'one more shared fact' rule.

what_we_take: The durable runner for searches: one workflow run per search with a step per web search, page read and extraction, getWritable() to push card updates, run.getReadable({startIndex}) so a staff member who leaves and reopens a running search picks up from the last chunk, and the local world (filesystem, zero config) for laptop prototypes with the Postgres world (Graphile Worker on our own Postgres) after that.

Adopt one durable engine only: this one beats Inngest, Trigger.dev and Hatchet on moving parts; against DBOS (from another batch) it wins on dev setup and confirmed resumable streams, and loses only if the team writes the pipeline in Python, where the Workflow SDK is labelled beta.

name: DBOS Transact (Python)
requirements_served: NFR effort and quality (per-search time and cost)
POC lesson: no short execution limit, parallel page reads
what_we_take: The library as is: one @DBOS.workflow per search (workflow id = search id), @DBOS.step per web search or page read, a DBOS queue with a concurrency limit for parallel reads, write_stream for partial person-card patches, and SQLite as the system DB on the laptop.
why: It fixes the POC's main failure (150 s Edge Function wall clock, serial 7 s seed searches) with no extra server, while Temporal needs a cluster and Inngest or Hatchet need a dev server, so it fits local-first prototyping best. read_stream takes an offset and has an async variant (read_stream_async), so a reopened search (F2) or a browser reconnect resumes from the last patch, and DBOS.sleep is durable for overnight runs. SQLite uses polling instead of LISTEN/NOTIFY; that is fine for 5 to 20 users, and Postgres later is only a change to the connection string.

name: Durable Streams protocol
what_we_take: The offset-and-replay pattern: each search writes an append-only event log (search_events with a monotonic id per search), the client reads from offset 0 on open or reload and then tails over SSE, resuming with Last-Event-ID, so a reopened search (F2) or an overnight run (F17) shows the same filled-in cards (F7).
why: The pattern matches how FN results arrive: people appear, then gain a name, role, ties and sources, and a search must be reopenable hours later. Running the protocol itself means a beta server (Node server 0.3.9 is dev-only; production needs the Caddy plugin) for 5 to 20 users, which a Postgres or SQLite table plus one SSE endpoint matches at a fraction of the moving parts. The same log also gives us the per-search time and cost record the NFR asks for.

name: Braintrust autoevals (semantic list-contains) and Braintrust pricing
requirements_served: Gold-set scoring: recall of known picks (differentiator)
POC lesson: every AI step checked against the gold set on each change
what_we_take: The ListContains algorithm. It finds the best one-to-one match between the gold picks and the returned people with scipy linear_sum_assignment over a pairwise similarity matrix. With allow_extra_entities=True it scores recall. We swap the default Levenshtein comparer for our duplicate rule (shared identifier, or name variant plus one shared fact).
why: The finding's claims are wrong. Matching is defined: Hungarian assignment with Levenshtein as the default. By default it does penalize extra items, because the denominator is max(len(outputs), len(expecteds)). That default gives the wrong number for FN, where a search returns 20 people and a case has 1 to 8 gold picks, so recall mode plus a separate top-5 human or LLM precision judgement is right. Levenshtein would miss 'Niko' versus 'Nikolai' the same way the POC did. The assignment step is about 15 lines, which beats adding autoevals plus scipy as a dependency. Drop the hosted platform: self-hosting is Enterprise only, Starter keeps data 14 days, and K5 does not need it for 28 cases kept in a local file.

name: Hard-group web recall sweep: Exa MCP vs Parallel MCP on 16 gold cases (74 picks)
what_we_take: The scoring protocol for the bake-off harness (round-1 borrow of the Exa people-search harness): three phrasings per case (Q verbatim, C event or company first, E employer named as a ceiling, never counted as discovery), a per-pick split into 'found only on the same event's record' vs 'found on an independent page', and a rule that the event's own record page (program PDF, host LinkedIn post, delegation event page) is excluded from the domain or URL set before recall is counted. Report recall with and without that exclusion.
why: This is a probe of two round-1 contenders (Exa MCP benchmark, Parallel MCP benchmark), not a new option, so it gets no adopt or benchmark of its own. Its value is the method and one finding that changes how we score: 33 of Exa's 44 Q hits sit only on the record of the same event, so raw recall measures precedent lookup, not discovery. Without the held-out-record rule every web contender will look better on the gold set than it will on a new question. The company-first miss on GS-03 (0 of 7 in both backends) also shows that business asks need a company list step before people search; that list does not exist in any state source (see the Georgia fact sheet).
beats_or_loses_to: Adds a scoring rule to the round-1 Exa people-search harness borrow; does not replace any round-1 pick. On these 16 cases Exa MCP beats Parallel MCP on event phrasings (Q+C 63 vs 17 of 74, pooled top 30), Parallel MCP is faster (median 1.0 s vs 1.9 s).

name: Exa keyless MCP rate limit behaviour
what_we_take: One adapter rule: an Exa response with HTTP 200 and a rateLimited flag in the body counts as a failed call, is retried with backoff (4 s or more), and is logged as a failure in the Search record, never scored as zero results. Pace keyless Exa at about one call per second in the Quick tier.
why: Without this rule the harness reads a rate-limited call as a miss and lowers Exa's recall without saying why, and the round-1 harness counts failures as zero. It is a few lines in the adapter. The deep tier fans out many calls and needs a key anyway, which the MVP already plans for (paid usage per the POC lessons).

Its one unique output is a self-reported nationality field. That field gives Bailet a "none" tie (Canada), which changes no pick. Being free and keyless does not save it, since it adds no gold pick that an adopted lane misses.

rerate.judge_note: Confirmed from saved probes: captions.list returned 403 and captions.download returned 401 without credentials. Download works only on videos the caller can edit, so it returns no text for Trouet (GS-28) or Sweldens (GS-02). The main failure is K2: there is no quotable third-party transcript. It also starts from a video id (K1). Topic web search already returns the YouTube talk URLs, for example 5 for Trouet through keyless Exa.
rerate.verifier_reason:
The drop holds. I checked this against the saved doc pages and probes. The captions.download page says the method "requires the user to have permission to edit the video" and costs 200 units. The captions.list page says the response "does not contain the actual captions" and costs 50 units. Both pages ask for the OAuth scope youtube.force-ssl or youtubepartner. So even with a token from a Google account, the API returns no text for a third-party talk such as Trouet's (GS-28) or Sweldens' (GS-02). That fails K2, because there is no quotable transcript. It also fails K5, because the token needs a personal login.

The probes agree with the docs. captions.list without a key returned 403 for unregistered callers. captions.download returned 401 CREDENTIALS_MISSING, with the message that an OAuth 2 token was expected.

One part of the rating is overstated. K1 is weak here: an enricher can take a video id from topic search, and K1 judges the query entry point, not each tool. Dropping the K1 point does not save the item.

It also adds nothing in the weak groups. Business founders (GS-03, GS-08, GS-22, GS-33), creatives (GS-11, GS-12, GS-21, GS-30) and low-footprint people (GS-24, GS-31) are not on videos FN can edit, so the API returns zero picks for them. The comparison route also checks out. The keyless Exa probe file holds 5 distinct Trouet video ids (He2KcvaDaDk, awKR0hBePNU, mLQ9kVx6Pfg, rnJKCEr1Hgk, w0nYj61Ky64) and dates including 2022-10-06. Topic web search therefore already covers talk discovery.

Nothing is worth borrowing either. Reading YouTube's unofficial timedtext endpoint would be a separate scraping route, not this API.

rerate.verifier_reason:
The drop holds because Podcast Index duplicates the iTunes call. I checked this in the saved spec, probes/i23-pi_api.json (v1.12.1). search/byperson takes a name and returns episodes, which is the job the keyless iTunes podcastEpisode call already does. byterm, bytitle and the keyless /search return only feeds, matched on the feed's title, author or owner. No endpoint takes a topic and returns people or guests, so the API fails K1 as a discovery source. The persons field exists only per feed or episode (episodes/byfeedurl), and using it would mean the per-show crawl the MVP rejected.

One fact in the rating is wrong. The spec documents a keyless route: /search, tagged "Apple Replacement", with security [] and "No API key needed". I called it on 2026-10-29, one call per term, 1 s apart:
- "Avery Trufelman" returned HTTP 200 and 2 feeds (Articles of Interest). iTunes already finds her for GS-21.
- "Pieter Trogh" returned 0, so it does not fix the C-01 iTunes miss at feed level.
- "ocean governance" returned 1 feed whose author is the show itself, not a person, so it gives GS-24 no gold pick.

No gold pick is gained in the weak groups:
- Business (GS-03, GS-08, GS-22, GS-33): picks such as Paul De Cock, Simon Lemmy and Christian Höferle can only be looked up by name, after another source has found them.
- Creative (GS-11, GS-12, GS-21, GS-30): feed-author matching equals the iTunes podcast entity search, which is keyless.
- Low footprint (GS-24, GS-31): the GS-24 probe returned no person.

The edge of byperson searching episode descriptions for Trogh, Martens and Lievens is still unmeasured. The keyed endpoints returned 401 (verified in probes/i23-nokey-headers.txt). The ToS 5.1 caching note in mvp-tech-reference.md no longer fails anything under the new K6 rule, and the rating rightly does not rely on it. A free key behind an hCaptcha signup is a developer account, not a personal licence. That counts against value, not as a K5 failure. Keep the key-probe plan on file with its 8-of-10 bar.

- Vervloesem, GS-03/04 (OMP 2023)
- Joris, GS-08 (3DPOD 2020)
- D'Hulst, GS-08 (2025)
- Trufelman, GS-21

name: Taddy Podcast API (GraphQL, full-text episode search, transcripts)
what_we_take: Nothing. Its one job in FN, a dated episode record per candidate found by full name, is already done by the keyless iTunes podcastEpisode call plus FN's own full-name and employer filter.
why: Taddy's own search docs say search matches only the episode name, description and creator fields, and "the transcript text is not searched". So it searches the same metadata iTunes does, and the "full-text and transcripts" label does not hold for search. It needs an X-USER-ID and X-API-KEY (a live keyless call returned HTTP 401 API_KEY_INVALID). The free plan allows 500 requests a month, Pro costs $75 a month for 100,000 requests and 100 generated transcripts, and the MVP needs neither transcripts nor webhooks, so per-person evidence costs more than iTunes and adds no claim type. As a topic-first source it only matches podcast titles and show notes, and topic web search (Parallel or Exa) already reaches those pages.

rerate.verifier_reason: The duplicate knockout holds. I re-read the saved Taddy search doc (probes/i36-developers_podcast-api_search.html). It says search matches the name, description, creators "and other relevant fields", and that "the transcript text is not searched". An episode that covers a topic only in audio therefore does not match. That is the same metadata the keyless iTunes podcastEpisode call already searches, by full name or by topic term. EXACT_PHRASE matching only moves FN's existing full-name filter to the server. It adds no recall. I re-fetched taddy.org/developers/pricing live on 2026-10-29 and the figures match: Free $0 for 500 requests a month, Pro $75 for 100,000 requests and 100 transcripts, Business $150 for 350,000 requests and 2,000 transcripts. The search doc URL returned HTTP 200. The saved probe file shows the keyless call answered HTTP 401 API_KEY_INVALID. The developer sign-up is self-serve and API-key sign-ups do not fail K5 elsewhere in this run, so K5 is not why it drops. It drops because it duplicates iTunes, costs more and adds no claim type. Against the weak groups: the business cases (GS-03, GS-08, GS-22, GS-33) and the low-footprint cases (GS-24, GS-31) pick founders, executives and scientists. The rater's comparison found no title or description match for the hard-group names in podcast metadata (Luc Martens 0 of 37 results, Bieke Zaman 0 of 19). Taddy searches the same fields, so it cannot reach spoken-only mentions either. In the creative group, the one podcast-native pick is Avery Trufelman in GS-21, and iTunes already finds her. Valerie Steele, Brandon Wen and Julie Kegels are reached through the web. GS-11, GS-12 and GS-30 are not a podcast-metadata problem. Taddy has one capability iTunes lacks: it returns a transcript for an episode that has one. But that works only after the episode is found through metadata, generated transcripts need Pro, and the MVP's claim types are already met by show notes. I made no keyed test, because the run's hard rules forbid accounts and keys. So the claim that Taddy finds no extra gold picks is still an inference, but every documented mechanism points the same way.

name: Podscan API (transcript search with extracted guests)

It publishes about 20 calls a minute, while Spotify's quota buckets are unpublished and "subject to change". key_probe_plan: A probe would need a Spotify account with Premium and a Development Mode app; the Client Credentials flow then gives a token. With that token, run GET /v1/search?type=episode&market=US&limit=10 by full name for the 10 gold names that were used for the iTunes count, including Avery Trufelman (GS-21) and Wim Sweldens (GS-02). That comes to about 10 to 20 calls at under 1 per second. Compare the hits against iTunes, keeping only episodes whose description names the employer or topic. Spotify earns a row only if it finds an episode for a gold pick that iTunes misses. The probe costs a Premium subscription, about $12 a month, and it fails K5 anyway, so it is not worth running.

rerate.judge_note: The saved quota-modes page confirms that a Development Mode app needs its owner to hold Spotify Premium. That is a personal paid member account, which fails K5. Search is capped at 10 results per call, against up to 200 from iTunes. No gold case depends on a Spotify-only show. Pulling a web-player token would get around Spotify's auth, so it was rightly not attempted.
rerate.verifier_reason:
The drop holds on two separate grounds, and either one is enough. First, the knockout is real. I re-read the saved quota-modes page, and a live fetch on 2026-10-29 returned HTTP 200. It says "The app owner must have a Spotify Premium account for apps in development mode to function." The February 2026 migration guide says the app stops working if the owner's Premium lapses. Extended quota is open only to organizations with at least 250k MAU (since 2025-05-15). The Search reference shows limit "Range: 0 - 10". The saved 401 response confirms there is no keyless route.

The strongest attack is that Premium is a paid self-serve plan at a published price, which passes K5. It fails anyway. Premium is a consumer subscription on a personal Spotify member account, and the API needs a registered personal Spotify login. That is exactly the member-account and personal-login case that still fails K5. Pulling the web player's anonymous token would get around Spotify's auth, so that route is out.

Second, even if K5 passed, it duplicates iTunes podcastEpisode. Both return episode title, description and release date, and both search by full name or keyword. iTunes is keyless and returns up to 200 results per call, against Spotify's 10. Most Spotify podcast catalog comes from public RSS feeds that Apple also indexes, so Spotify adds no new claim type.

The weak groups do not rescue it. Business cases GS-03, GS-08, GS-22 and GS-33 need Belgian ties and US location, which episode metadata does not carry. Creative cases GS-11, GS-12, GS-21 and GS-30 rest on Avery Trufelman's Articles of Interest (GS-21) and similar shows, which are on Apple too. Low-footprint cases GS-24 and GS-31 are by definition people with few appearances. A 10-result keyword search over episodes cannot find new people in those groups better than iTunes keyword search, which has 20 times the page size. No gold pick has been shown to appear only on a Spotify-exclusive show.

One correction to the record: the reference doc (line 886) still gives the old reason, that the Developer Policy bans AI ingestion. That is terms, and terms no longer fail K6 on their own. The rater's new K5 and duplicate reasons are the ones that hold. The about $12 a month Premium price is plausible but I did not re-check it, and it does not change the verdict.

The drop holds. I re-read the seven saved probe pages. The publiq project page describes data sharing between data producers (the public) and data consumers (culture venues). The 2023 detail page says authentication runs through the government's ACM/IDM. The 6 Oct 2026 legal article lists the onboarding steps: the organisation joins, its staff register, the provider makes a dataset available, and access is requested and granted. That same article says datasets can contain pseudonymised personal data and that re-identifying anyone is forbidden. So the platform is built to stop exactly the person lookup FN needs. I also found something the rater missed. uitwisselingsplatform.be redirects to a data-product-management app. Its JS bundle names catalog.uitwisselingsplatform.be, a Jupyter host, Keycloak OpenID Connect sign-in and registration routes, and the endpoints /api/register/user, /api/organisation/is-registered and /api/output-ports/access-requests. That points to a dataset catalogue behind registration plus access requests, which confirms K5. I tried plain GETs on /api/data-product and the catalogue host, but the permission system blocked them, so I cannot say whether the catalogue listing itself is public. Even if it were, it would list audience and ticketing datasets, not people.

Wikidata labels P5068 "Flanders Arts Institute person ID (former scheme)" and P12674 "Kunstenpunt Knowledge Graph ID". kunsten.be, updated 27 Oct 2026, still says the transfer of the Arts Database to the platform is only being explored. Exports stay open until Dec 2027, and the database's last data updates were April and September 2026.

- Creative (GS-11, GS-12, GS-21, GS-30): there are no person records today. If Arts Database people do move over, the Wikidata Kunstenpunt ids already reach them without a key.
- Low footprint (GS-24 marine scientists, GS-31 LA AI and media): out of the platform's domain.

name: K6 verdict table and own-fetch pipeline rule (web backends, storing quote + URL + date)
requirements_served: Data model: Claim (tie claims reused across searches)
what_we_take: One pipeline rule for every web backend: the provider only finds candidate URLs; FN re-fetches the page itself (httpx + trafilatura, Firecrawl as fallback), and the claim row stores quote_exact, URL and retrieved_at from that fetch. Provider excerpts, Basis reasoning and snippets are never stored as claim text. One written question goes to Parallel and Exa before the gold-set run, and the replies are kept in the repo. The verdict changes: Parallel stays adopt under this rule, Exa becomes benchmark-only, Perplexity stays benchmark on name-free queries, You.com stays benchmark on web results, Firecrawl stays adopt, Brave and Tavily stay dropped.
why: The MVP data model reuses tie claims across searches (F2, Claim), and that reuse is what both Parallel 2(c)(xi) and Exa 4.2(a) restrict. Quoting from our own fetch moves the quote and date out of the provider contract. The only provider-derived thing left in the database is a URL string, and the written request covers that. One correction to the table: Parallel 2(b)(i) bans storing Output for other End Customers (the Customer's own customers). FN's staff are Authorized Users (1(a)), so 2(b)(i) does not block internal display. The real risks are 2(c)(vi)(B) ('create databases') and 2(c)(xi). Second correction: a benchmark run that writes Exa results to disk for scoring is already 'copy' under Exa 4.2(a). Round 2 has done this (round2/r_e_*.json), so the Exa letter has to go out before the formal gold-set run, not after it.

key_probe_plan: With an Exa key on the $10 monthly free credit, run sub-arm B-people on all 28 scorable cases. I checked i34-summary-raw.txt: on GS-02 as typed, Vetter came back at rank 3 and Baeyens at rank 4, from linkedin.com profiles that do not mention the event, each with a dated KU Leuven or Ghent education. That beats arm B, which got 33 of its 44 hits from event pages. It runs on the arm B key, so there is no new account, and it costs about $0.047 a call, under $5 for the gold set. It found 1 of 7 on GS-03 and missed De Cock and Vervloesem even with the employer named, and that gap is why the structured arm (i39) runs beside it. Tie typing reads educationHistory and workHistory only, never the publishedDate crawl date.
rerate.verifier_reason: The benchmark verdict holds. I re-checked the key facts live on 2026-10-29. (1) The changelog at exa.ai/docs/changelog.md (HTTP 200) says the people category replaced linkedin and covers "1B+ public profiles", "across the whole web, not just LinkedIn". (2) exa.ai/versus/perplexity still says "1B+ LinkedIn profiles with 50M+ updates per week". The probe shows that 200 of 200 results were linkedin.com, so the LinkedIn reading is the one that matches the data. (3) The spec still lists category people. It rejects excludeDomains with a 400 and ignores domain filters. (4) The Search quickstart says lite accepts every category, people included, at the lite price, so the Quick tier is valid. (5) The probe log holds real person entities. Baeyens has KU Leuven PhD 1992-1997 and Nokia Bell Labs from 2022-01-01, plus a public exa.ai/library/person id. That meets K2 under the new vendor-record rule, and tie typing can read educationHistory rather than the Exa company blurb ('presence in France, Belgium'). (6) On GS-02 as typed, Vetter came back at rank 3 and Baeyens at rank 4, from profiles that do not mention the event. On GS-03, only Vantieghem was found, on the profile phrasing. (7) Pricing is pay-as-you-go with a $10 monthly free credit and no card. Arm B already has the key, so K5 passes with no sales call. Attack results: this arm does not beat OpenAlex on GS-02, which found 3 of 3 academic picks. On GS-03 it loses to EDGAR for De Cock. Its real case is held-out finds that come with dated tie records in the groups where structured lanes are weak. Vantieghem on GS-03 is one example: neither EDGAR nor OpenAlex would reach a chamber president. That makes it a credible contender, not an adopt, which is what benchmark means. The cost note is wrong but in the safe direction. On /search, only AI page summaries are billed on top. Text is not billed per page there, since the $1/1k-pages rate applies to /contents. So an auto call with 25 results is about $0.007 + $0.015 = $0.022, not $0.047, and the benchmark costs less than stated. Most gold_cases_helped entries marked "expected" (GS-09, GS-08, GS-01, GS-31, GS-13, GS-32, GS-11, GS-18) were not probed. Treat them as hypotheses for the key run, not as findings.

beats_or_loses_to: It beats Parallel Search, Exa Search (web, linkedin.com excluded) and FindAll on structured alumni-in-metro queries and on dated education tie claims for business people. EDGAR finds only officers of public companies and Form D founders. It loses to OpenAlex and FRIS on academics and Flanders-based researchers, and to the seed lists on Instant speed. It has no topic boundary beyond LinkedIn keyword matching, so precision on vague topics (GS-10 "any research field", GS-12 Jan Yoors) should be poor. Against its sibling, the Exa people category (same LinkedIn origin), it should win on exact school, location and company filters and lose on semantic topic queries. The group judge picks between them on the benchmark.

key_probe_plan: The probe needs an Apify Starter account ($19/month, which covers the spend) and an APIFY_TOKEN loaded from Keychain inline. Use harvestapi/linkedin-profile-search through run-sync-get-dataset-items. Step 1 is two cases, about 10 runs and about $1.50. GS-09 runs searchQuery "tax OR legal OR subsidiary" with schools [Vlerick Business School, KU Leuven] and location United States. Each run uses takePages 2 in Full mode. Record wall time per run against the POC's 3.4 s and 17 s, picks in the top 50 (Baeyens, Vetter, Sweldens, Klein; Segers, Troch, Van Velzen), and whether education and experience dates come back. Step 2 runs only if step 1 finds at least 2 of 4 GS-02 picks or Segers: run it as an arm next to B on all 28 cases at Quick. That is about 3 queries per case and 50 full profiles, about $0.50 a case and $15 in all, scored on held-out recall in the hard groups (business GS-03, GS-08, GS-22, GS-32; low footprint GS-31) and on tie-label accuracy from education claims. Also run harvestapi/linkedin-profile-scraper by profile URL ($0.004 a profile) as the EDGAR-step tie lookup for business picks found by other lanes.
